title: Sustainability and Business Practices
text:
Welcome
This book is the lecture-note companion for MGMT-3105 – Sustainability and Business Practices, a second-year course that introduces the philosophy of sustainability and the discipline of project management to students in electromechanical and mechanical engineering technology programs.
You are training for careers in the automotive, food-processing, and defense industries. In every one of those sectors you will, sooner than you expect, be handed a slice of a project: a line retrofit, a new product introduction, a validation campaign, a plant move. This course is about the structure that keeps such work on scope, on schedule, and on budget — and about doing it in a way that does not quietly borrow from the future to pay for the present.

title: Sustainability and Business Practices
section: Why a course that pairs sustainability with project management?
text:
Why a course that pairs sustainability with project management?
At first glance they look like two subjects stapled together. They are not. Every project consumes resources — materials, energy, money, human effort — and every project leaves something behind: a product, a process, a waste stream, a set of habits in the organization. Project management is the set of tools that decides how those resources are spent, and sustainability is the lens that asks whether that spend was worth it beyond the next quarter. A project manager who can build a work breakdown structure but cannot reason about lifecycle impact is only doing half the job.

title: Sustainability and Business Practices
text:
The running project
Throughout the book we return to one worked scenario, taken from the MGMT-3105 term project: your company designs and manages the launch of a 1/18-scale radio-controlled vehicle replica for the toy market, then wins a contract to manufacture 100 000+ units for the following holiday season. You choose the vehicle, the body and frame materials (steel, aluminium, or carbon fibre), and one of two Canadian motor/control-system suppliers. Every chapter uses a piece of that project — its scope, its WBS, its schedule, its budget, its risks, its closeout — so the tools connect to a single concrete thing rather than a dozen disconnected examples.

How the book is organized
Each chapter opens with measurable learning objectives and a real-world hook, develops the theory with plain-language explanations and LaTeX equations, and illustrates it with R-generated figures. Worked examples are shown step by step; wherever an example is a self-contained calculation, it is offered as a live, editable R cell you can run and modify in your browser. Collapsible Practice and Discussion blocks let you test yourself before revealing the answer, and each chapter closes with curated YouTube videos for a second explanation in a different voice.

Define sustainability and sustainable design, and explain the three pillars (social, economic, ecological) and the “triple bottom line.”
Identify the four points of the sustainability platform — recycling, bio-based/biodegradable polymers, material reduction, and design for recyclability — and give an engineering example of each.

Before we begin: think of the last thing you threw away today

Where did its materials come from? How long did you use it before it became waste? Where is it now — landfill, recycling stream, incinerator? Could a different design decision, made years ago by an engineer you will never meet, have changed that answer? Keep the object in mind; we will come back to it.

title: 1  Sustainability
section: 1.2 Introduction: every gram, multiplied by a hundred thousand
text:
1.2 Introduction: every gram, multiplied by a hundred thousand
Here is the situation that runs through this whole book. Your company designs and manages the launch of a 1/18-scale radio-controlled vehicle replica for the toy market. If the prototype is accepted, you win a contract to build 100 000+ units for the next holiday season. Early on, you must choose the body material — steel, aluminium, or carbon fibre — and the frame material — aluminium or carbon fibre.
That single choice is not just a strength-and-weight problem. Multiply it by 100 000 units and it becomes a decision about:

how many tonnes of raw material leave the ground,
how many megajoules of energy are spent turning that material into parts,
how much scrap and packaging waste the line produces every shift,
whether the finished toy can be recycled when a child outgrows it in three years,
and whether your customer — a large retailer with its own public sustainability targets — will even put it on the shelf.

This is why sustainability belongs at the front of a project-management course, not tacked on at the end. The tools you meet in later chapters — scope, WBS, schedule, budget, risk — all decide how resources get spent. Sustainability is the question of whether that spend was worth it once you look past the launch date.






Note



Industry snapshot. General Motors’ CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ontario — an hour from where this course is taught — runs landfill-free: every waste stream from daily operations is reused, recycled, or converted to energy. That is not a marketing slogan bolted onto an existing plant; it is a set of thousands of small design and process decisions of exactly the kind this chapter is about.

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.3 What sustainability means
The most quoted definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland report and is used almost word-for-word by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency:

Sustainability is “meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.”

The idea is older than the word. Thomas Jefferson expressed the same principle in financial terms: do not leave a debt for future generations to pay. Swap “debt” for “depleted resources, degraded ecosystems, and accumulated waste” and you have the modern version.
Sustainable design applies that principle to the things engineers actually produce. Wikipedia’s working definition is useful: the philosophy of designing physical objects, the built environment, and services to comply with the principles of social, economic, and ecological sustainability. The intent is to minimize negative environmental impact through skilful, sensitive design while holding a dynamic balance between economy and society.

1.3.1 The three pillars and the triple bottom line
Sustainability is usually drawn as three overlapping domains. A decision is sustainable only where all three overlap: it has to be socially acceptable, economically viable, and ecologically sound at the same time.

circles <- data.frame(
  x0 = c(-0.55, 0.55, 0),
  y0 = c(0.35, 0.35, -0.6),
  r  = rep(1.05, 3),
  pillar = c("Social\n(bearable)", "Economic\n(viable)", "Ecological\n(sound)"),
  fill = c("#2E86C1", "#F39C12", "#27AE60")
)

ggplot(circles) +
  ggforce::geom_circle(aes(x0 = x0, y0 = y0, r = r, fill = fill),
                       alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.8, color = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  annotate("text", x = -0.95, y = 0.9, label = "SOCIAL",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#1B4F72") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.95, y = 0.9, label = "ECONOMIC",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#9C640C") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -1.55, label = "ECOLOGICAL",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#186A3B") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.55, label = "bearable",
           size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.7, y = -0.35, label = "equitable",
           size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.7, y = -0.35, label = "viable",
           size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "italic") +

  labs(title = "Sustainability lives in the overlap") +

  theme(

Figure 1.1: The three pillars of sustainability. Only decisions in the central overlap are genuinely sustainable; the pairwise overlaps (bearable, equitable, viable) each miss one dimension.







Discussion: which pillar does each of these decisions serve — and which does it ignore?


A supplier offers motors 20 % cheaper, made in a plant with a poor safety record. (economic yes; social no)
You switch the body to recycled aluminium, adding $0.40 per unit. (ecological yes; economic maybe)
You keep an inefficient old assembly line running because retraining staff on a new one is disruptive. (social short-term yes; ecological and economic long-term no)

The point of the diagram is that a “win” on one pillar is not a win. You have to check all three.

title: 1  Sustainability
section: 1.4 The four points of the sustainability platform
text:
1.4 The four points of the sustainability platform
For a product engineer, sustainability comes down to four levers:

Recycling — can the material be recovered and used again?
Bio-based or biodegradable polymers — can the material come from a renewable source, or return safely to the environment?
Material reduction — can the product do its job with less material in the first place?
Designing for recyclability — is the product built so that recovery is actually practical, not just theoretically possible?

The rest of the chapter takes these one at a time, then widens out to what sustainability means when you are managing a whole project rather than designing one part.

1.4.1 Sustainable design principles
The design literature expands the four levers into a set of working principles:







Principle
What it means in practice




Low-impact materials
Non-toxic, sustainably produced or recycled materials that need less energy to process.


Energy efficiency
Choose manufacturing processes — and design products — that require less energy over their life.


Emotionally durable design
Build things people want to keep. A product kept for ten years instead of three cuts consumption and waste by more than any recycling scheme.


Design for reuse and recycling
Design for a commercial “afterlife” — but without compromising performance or service life to get there. It is a balancing act.



Notice the tension already built in: “make it last” and “make it recyclable” pull in opposite directions, and “use less material” can fight “make it durable.” Good sustainable design is the art of resolving those tensions, not pretending they do not exist.

Two grades of recyclate matter to a manufacturer:

Post-industrial (a.k.a. regrind): clean scrap from your own or a supplier’s process — runners, sprues, start-up shots, off-spec parts. Easy to reuse because you know exactly what it is.
Post-consumer: material that has been through a consumer’s hands. It must be collected, sorted, washed, ground, and often re-pelletized, and it can carry metal, labels, food residue, and other polymers. Much harder to work with, but it is the stream that actually diverts waste from landfill.



Think about it: your RC-car body is moulded from a glass-filled ABS/PC blend. Which recycling code does it carry, and what does that tell you?

It carries #7 (OTHER) — any multi-polymer blend or filled material that is not one of codes 1–6 lands here. In practice, #7 is rarely recycled through curbside programs: the blend cannot be melted back into a single clean polymer. If recyclability matters for this product, that is a signal to reconsider the material before tooling is cut, not after.

title: 1  Sustainability
section: 1.6 Recyclable vs. biodegradable: a real tension
text:
1.6 Recyclable vs. biodegradable: a real tension
Years ago the plastics industry pursued two waste strategies at once — recycling and biodegradability — and they turned out to be partly opposed. If you make a part from recyclate and want it to last (think plastic lumber, or a pallet), the last thing you want is biodegradable material mixed in, causing the part to fail early. Contaminate a recycling stream with enough compostable polymer and the whole batch can become unusable.
The industry chose recycling. But with fossil-fuel prices and supply security back in the spotlight, biopolymers have returned. Some of the earliest plastics were bio-based (cellulosics, natural rubber); many new ones are built from corn or potato starch. Polylactic acid (PLA) is made from corn starch and behaves a lot like PET, but it is harder to process and degrades faster at elevated temperature.
And “biodegradable” has an asterisk. Degradation is done by microbes, which need oxygen and moisture. A modern landfill is compacted, dry, and low-oxygen — almost nothing degrades well there. You can dig up decades-old newspaper and still read it.






Important



Case study — EcoPlast Packaging (MGMT-3105, Week 1). EcoPlast launched corn-based PLA food containers. Then: customers found them brittle in the cold and warped in heat; recyclers reported PLA contaminating conventional-plastic batches; consumers wanted eco-friendly and the same durability as regular plastic; and environmental groups argued the containers mostly ended up in landfill, where they did not meaningfully biodegrade — calling it “green marketing.”




Discussion (Week 1 case): was it unreasonably risky for EcoPlast to trade durability for sustainability, and what would you change?

Model answer. A product that fails in real-world use creates more waste, erodes consumer trust, and undermines the point of sustainability — so yes, the trade-off as executed was unreasonably risky. Consumers share some responsibility for unrealistic expectations, but the company had a duty to manage those expectations and to test properly before launch. Rushing to market compromised quality.
What to change: (1) real R&D and performance testing across the actual temperature and handling range before launch; (2) an accurate caution label (“not suitable for hot liquids”) — a danger label would be excessive; (3) consumer education on correct disposal (industrial compost, not curbside or landfill); (4) stop marketing the product as fully “sustainable” until there is evidence of an environmental benefit in real disposal conditions — otherwise the claim is exposed to a misleading-marketing challenge.

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.7 Material reduction
Reducing the material that goes into a product — at the design stage, by thinning walls, removing bosses, right-sizing ribs, or substituting a lighter material — pays off several times over:

the product costs less (less material bought per unit),
there is less to recycle or dispose of at end of life,
more material is left for other uses,
and less energy is spent producing and transporting every unit.

The catch: you cannot thin your way past the product’s functional requirements. Material reduction is enabled by better material properties, better processes, and better analysis — not by wishful thinking.

1.7.1 Worked Example 1: thinning the RC-car body
Your baseline RC-car body is injection-moulded ABS with a mass of 48 g. Simulation says you can drop the nominal wall from 2.5 mm to 2.1 mm and still pass the drop test, cutting body mass to 41 g. The contract run is 120 000 units. ABS costs $3.10/kg, its production embodied energy is about 90 MJ/kg, and its cradle-to-gate carbon intensity is about 3.4 kg CO2e/kg.

mass_before_g <- 48
mass_after_g  <- 41
units         <- 120000
abs_cost_per_kg   <- 3.10
abs_energy_MJ_kg  <- 90
abs_co2e_kg_kg    <- 3.4

saved_kg <- (mass_before_g - mass_after_g) / 1000 * units

cost_saved   <- saved_kg * abs_cost_per_kg
energy_saved <- saved_kg * abs_energy_MJ_kg
co2_saved    <- saved_kg * abs_co2e_kg_kg

cat("Mass removed per unit :", mass_before_g - mass_after_g, "g\n")
cat("Material saved over the run :", format(round(saved_kg), big.mark = " "), "kg\n")
cat("Material cost saved :", sprintf("$%s", format(round(cost_saved), big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("Production energy saved :", format(round(energy_saved), big.mark = " "), "MJ",
    sprintf("(~%s kWh)", format(round(energy_saved / 3.6), big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("Cradle-to-gate CO2e avoided :", format(round(co2_saved), big.mark = " "), "kg",
    sprintf("(~%.1f t)", co2_saved / 1000), "\n")

Mass removed per unit : 7 g
Material saved over the run : 840 kg
Material cost saved : $2 604 
Production energy saved : 75 600 MJ (~21 000 kWh) 
Cradle-to-gate CO2e avoided : 2 856 kg (~2.9 t) 


A 7 g decision, taken once on a screen, moves almost a tonne of material and several tonnes of CO2e once it is multiplied by the production run — before counting the lighter shipping weight.


1.7.2 Try it yourself: the material-choice decision
Now compare the three candidate body materials head to head. The live cell below holds rough figures for steel, aluminium, and carbon-fibre composite bodies of the mass each material would need for equal stiffness. Change the numbers, add a recycled-content option, or change the run size and see what happens to cost, energy, and carbon.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


What the numbers usually show — and why the “greenest” answer is not obvious

Carbon fibre gives the lightest body, which cuts shipping energy and, in a real vehicle, fuel over the whole service life. But its production energy and carbon per kilogram are the highest of the three, and it is the hardest to recycle (code #7, thermoset matrix). Steel is cheap and highly recycled but heavy. Aluminium sits in between and is excellent if you can get recycled stock — secondary aluminium uses roughly 5 % of the energy of primary.
For a toy that is shipped once and never driven under its own power for thousands of kilometres, the use-phase fuel saving from carbon fibre never arrives — so the decision tilts back toward recycled aluminium or steel. The lesson: the right material depends on where the impact actually lands in the life cycle.

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.8 Designing for recyclability
Recyclability is designed in, not hoped for. The checklist a plastics engineer can actually influence:

Make the assembly from a single material, or from compatible materials that can be recycled together.
Make it easy to disassemble.
Prefer snap-fits and press-fits over screws and metal fasteners.
Reduce the part count.
Avoid labels (or use same-polymer labels / in-mould labelling).
Keep thermosets out of thermoplastic assemblies — use thermoplastic elastomers instead of rubber seals where you can.

You may not have the final word on a design, but you can always offer the greener alternative. And the mindset has shifted: products used to be designed for end of life — last for period X, then done. Now good products are designed for next life: what can this material become after its first use?


Try it: redesign the RC-car battery door for recyclability

Current design: ABS door, two stainless M2 screws, a printed polyester label, a moulded-in TPE gasket (thermoset-like behaviour), a steel spring.
One redesign:

Replace the two screws with a living hinge + snap latch moulded into the door (same ABS) — removes two dissimilar-metal fasteners and a driver operation on the line.
Replace the adhesive polyester label with in-mould labelling in an ABS-compatible film, or mould the text into the part.
Replace the steel spring with a moulded ABS cantilever spring if the cycle life allows.
Keep the TPE gasket but make it a removable press-in part in a recycling-compatible grade, or switch to a moulded-in flexible ABS lip if the seal spec allows.

Result: the door goes from five materials and two fasteners to essentially one polymer, snaps apart by hand, and carries no adhesive.

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.9 The consumer’s perspective
Sustainable design has to survive contact with real buyers. Market research is consistent on two points:

Environmentally conscious consumers will pay marginally more and accept marginally lower fit and finish for a product that is genuinely more environmentally friendly.
They have zero tolerance for a drop in performance/functionality or in service life. They bought the product to do a job. If a “sustainable” design wears out sooner, it just gets replaced sooner — consuming more resources and defeating the purpose.


tol <- data.frame(
  attribute = c("Higher price", "Cosmetic fit & finish",
                "Core performance", "Service life / durability"),
  tolerance = c(0.55, 0.45, 0.03, 0.05)
)
tol$attribute <- factor(tol$attribute, levels = rev(tol$attribute))
tol$kind <- ifelse(tol$tolerance > 0.2, "Some tolerance", "Near-zero tolerance")

ggplot(tol, aes(x = tolerance, y = attribute, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(tolerance, accuracy = 1)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.7),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Some tolerance" = "#27AE60",
                               "Near-zero tolerance" = "#C0392B")) +
  labs(title = "Where consumers will --- and will not --- give ground",
       x = "Approximate share of consumers willing to accept a trade-off",
       y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 1.2: Consumer tolerance for trade-offs made in the name of sustainability: some room on price and cosmetics, essentially none on how well the product works or how long it lasts.






1.9.1 Whole-life cost: cheaper to buy vs. cheaper to own
This is where planned obsolescence enters. A business may have a commercial reason to limit a product’s life — it protects repeat sales. Sustainable design pushes the other way: make it last. The buyer’s own wallet is often on the side of durability, even when the sticker price is higher.
The live cell compares a cheap version of a product (low price, short life, replaced repeatedly) with a durable version (higher price, lasts the whole period). Change the prices, lifetimes, and horizon and watch which one wins on total cost of ownership — and on units sent to landfill.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Where does the cheap option actually win?

Shorten the horizon (you only need the product for a year), or make the durable version’s premium extreme relative to its extra life, and “cheap” wins on cost. But the waste count almost always favours durable: five landfilled units versus one. Whole-life thinking means putting both numbers — dollars and units — in front of the decision-maker, not just the sticker price.

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.10 Sustainability in project management
Everything above was about designing a part. When you are running a project, sustainability becomes a set of management actions spread across the whole life cycle. The MGMT-3105 checklist:
Procurement and contracts

Choose eco-friendly and ethical suppliers; audit them for compliance.
Put sustainability clauses in contracts.
Perform an Environmental & Social Impact Assessment (ESIA).

Design and materials

Minimize raw-material use; prioritize recyclable, renewable, and local resources.
Design for energy and water efficiency.
Apply circular-economy principles: reuse, refurbish, recycle.
Plan the product/service lifecycle — what happens to it after the project ends.

Operations

Reduce carbon emissions from transport and operations.
Use digital tools to cut paper and travel.
Run proper waste management: segregation, recycling, safe disposal.

People and governance

Safeguard health, safety, and well-being of the team and the community.
Support social responsibility: local hiring, fair wages, training.
Track sustainability KPIs: carbon footprint, waste-reduction %, energy saved.
Monitor suppliers and contractors; identify and mitigate environmental and social risks; run sustainability audits when needed.


1.10.1 The circular economy
The circular economy is the alternative to the linear take — make — use — dispose model. Instead, material is kept in use through loops of increasing size: maintain and reuse first, then refurbish and remanufacture, then recycle, with disposal as the last resort.

stages <- data.frame(
  label = c("Design", "Make", "Distribute", "Use", "Maintain / Reuse",
            "Refurbish / Remanufacture", "Recycle"),
  angle = seq(90, 90 - 360 + 360/7, length.out = 7) * pi / 180
)
stages$x <- cos(stages$angle)
stages$y <- sin(stages$angle)

seg <- data.frame(
  x    = stages$x,
  y    = stages$y,
  xend = stages$x[c(2:7, 1)],
  yend = stages$y[c(2:7, 1)]
)

ggplot() +
  geom_curve(data = seg, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
             curvature = -0.25, linewidth = 0.9, color = "#27AE60",
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_point(data = stages, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 20, color = "#EAF6EC") +
  geom_point(data = stages, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 20, shape = 1, color = "#27AE60") +
  geom_text(data = stages, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
            size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold",
            lineheight = 0.9, color = "grey15") +

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.11 Key Takeaways

Sustainability = meeting present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs. Sustainable design applies that across social, economic, and ecological pillars at once — a “win” on one pillar is not a win.
The four levers for a product engineer: recycle, bio-source/biodegrade, reduce material, design for recyclability.
The seven resin codes tell a sorter what a plastic is; PET (#1), HDPE (#2), and PP (#5) recycle well, #7 (blends/PLA/filled) rarely does. Post-consumer recyclate diverts real waste but is hard to process; post-industrial regrind is easy.
Recyclable and biodegradable can conflict, and “biodegradable” does little in a dry, compacted landfill — the EcoPlast case shows what happens when that asterisk is ignored.
A small material-reduction decision, multiplied by the production run, moves tonnes of material, energy, and CO2e. The “greenest” material depends on where in the life cycle the impact lands — use phase vs. production vs. end of life.
Consumers give ground on price and cosmetics but not on performance or durability; whole-life cost usually favours the durable design on both dollars and landfill count.
In project management, sustainability is a checklist across procurement, design, operations, and governance — backed by circular-economy loops and tracked with KPIs (carbon per unit, waste diversion, recycled content).

title: 1  Sustainability
text:
1.12 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Packaging substitution (food industry)

A food-processing client ships 2.4 million meal trays a year. The current tray is 22 g of black CPET (#1, but often rejected by sorters because black plastic is invisible to optical sorting). A proposed natural-coloured PP (#5) tray weighs 19 g, costs $0.006/g versus $0.005/g for the CPET, and is accepted by the client’s regional recycler.

What is the annual change in material mass and material cost?
Give two non-cost arguments for switching, and one argument against.

Solution.

trays        <- 2.4e6
mass_cpet_g  <- 22
mass_pp_g    <- 19
cost_cpet    <- 0.005
cost_pp      <- 0.006

mass_change_kg <- (mass_pp_g - mass_cpet_g) / 1000 * trays
cost_change    <- (mass_pp_g * cost_pp - mass_cpet_g * cost_cpet) * trays

cat("Annual material mass change :", format(round(mass_change_kg), big.mark = " "), "kg",
    "(a reduction)\n")
cat("Annual material cost change : ",
    sprintf("$%s", format(round(cost_change), big.mark = " ")),
    " (an increase)\n", sep = "")

Annual material mass change : -7 200 kg (a reduction)
Annual material cost change : $9 600 (an increase)



About 7 200 kg less plastic per year, but roughly $3 700/yr more spent on material because PP costs more per gram here and the 3 g saving does not fully offset it.
For: the natural-coloured PP is actually recovered by the recycler (black CPET usually is not), and PP trays tolerate reheating better. Against: higher material spend, and a tooling change is needed — capital plus a qualification run.




Problem 2: Recycled-aluminium body (automotive/toy)

Switching the RC-car body from primary to recycled aluminium keeps the mass at 70 g/unit but changes the cradle-to-gate energy from 155 MJ/kg to 8 MJ/kg and the carbon from 11 kg CO2e/kg to 0.6 kg CO2e/kg. Recycled stock costs $0.25/kg more. Run size 120 000 units.
Estimate the energy saved, the CO2e avoided, and the extra material cost.
Solution.

mass_kg   <- 70 / 1000
units     <- 120000
kg_total  <- mass_kg * units

energy_saved <- kg_total * (155 - 8)
co2_saved    <- kg_total * (11 - 0.6)
extra_cost   <- kg_total * 0.25

cat("Aluminium in the run :", format(round(kg_total), big.mark = " "), "kg\n")
cat("Production energy saved :", format(round(energy_saved), big.mark = " "), "MJ",
    sprintf("(~%s kWh)\n", format(round(energy_saved / 3.6), big.mark = " ")))
cat("CO2e avoided :", format(round(co2_saved), big.mark = " "), "kg",
    sprintf("(~%.1f t)\n", co2_saved / 1000))
cat("Extra material cost :",
    sprintf("$%s\n", format(round(extra_cost), big.mark = " ")))

Aluminium in the run : 8 400 kg
Production energy saved : 1 234 800 MJ (~343 000 kWh)
CO2e avoided : 87 360 kg (~87.4 t)
Extra material cost : $2 100


Roughly 1.2 million MJ (about 340 000 kWh) and 87 t of CO2e avoided for about $2 100 of extra material cost — one of the highest-leverage sustainability moves available on this project.



Problem 3: Design-for-recyclability audit (defense)

A defense client requires that field-returned electronic enclosures be materially recoverable. You are handed this enclosure: glass-filled nylon (#7) housing, 6 zinc-plated steel screws, a bonded aluminium RFI shield, a polyurethane potting compound over the PCB, and two adhesive asset-tracking labels.
List, in priority order, the four changes that would most improve material recovery, and note the functional risk of each.
Model answer.

Replace the potting compound with a removable conformal coating or a gasketed enclosure. Risk: reduced shock/moisture protection — must re-qualify to the environmental spec.
Eliminate the bonded aluminium shield; use a conductive coating on the nylon or a snap-in shield of the same-family metal. Risk: RFI performance must be re-verified.
Swap the 6 steel screws for moulded snap features or same-metal fasteners. Risk: fewer re-assembly cycles; captive-hardware requirement may forbid it.
Drop adhesive labels for moulded-in or laser-etched marking. Risk: contrast/legibility and traceability sign-off.

The housing polymer itself (#7 glass-filled) is hard to change if the structural spec depends on it — note it as a known limitation rather than a quick fix.



Problem 4 (discussion): planned obsolescence vs. sustainable design

“Sustainable design requires that our products last as long as possible. But business decisions may deliberately shorten product life to protect repeat sales — planned obsolescence. Which do you prefer, and how would you reconcile the two in a company that has to stay profitable?”
There is no single right answer — this is a position you argue. Strong answers usually land on service and circular business models: the manufacturer keeps revenue through repair, upgrades, refurbishment, take-back, or product-as-a-service, so “make it last” and “keep earning” stop being opposites. Weak answers just pick a side and ignore the constraint on the other.

text:
2.2 Introduction: only one project in four
Here is a sobering number that opens this course: by common industry estimates, only about 26 % of projects are delivered successfully while respecting the triple constraint — on scope, on time, on budget. The other three in four slip, overspend, descope, or fail outright.
That is why project management exists as a discipline. Running the RC-vehicle launch from the last chapter is not the same as running a production line. A line is a process: repetitive, permanent, tuned once and then kept stable. A project is a one-time push toward a unique goal, under a deadline and a budget, and it needs different tools and a different mindset.






Important



Case study — Orion Tech (MGMT-3105, Week 2). A software company built a healthcare app. The team was skilled, but: developers were never clear on requirements and reworked constantly; the PM ran everything through email and buried the team; stakeholders got no status reports; a few voices dominated meetings while others went silent; and tone and urgency were misread between the local team and offshore developers. Deadlines slipped, the budget grew, and the client’s satisfaction collapsed. Leadership asked whether the PM had followed any communication protocol at all.

Project

text:
2.4 The triple constraint
Every project is boxed in by scope, time, and cost, with quality sitting in the middle as the measure of whether stakeholders are satisfied. Resources (people, equipment, facilities) are the fourth practical limit.

tri <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 2, 4, 0),
  y = c(0, 3.4, 0, 0)
)
ggplot(tri, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "#5DADE2", alpha = 0.25, color = "#2E86C1", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 1.9, label = "SCOPE", angle = 60,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.2 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#1B4F72") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 1.9, label = "TIME", angle = -60,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.2 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#1B4F72") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = -0.28, label = "COST",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.2 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#1B4F72") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 1.15, label = "QUALITY",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#B03A2E") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0.72,
           label = "(stakeholder satisfaction)", fontface = "italic",
           size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, color = "grey35") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.6, 4.6), ylim = c(-0.7, 3.8)) +
  labs(title = "Pick two to fix; the third must flex") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale,
                                  face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))







Figure 2.1: The triple constraint. Scope, time, and cost form the sides; quality is the area they enclose. Change one side and at least one other must move, or quality suffers.







Think about it: the retailer moves the RC-vehicle launch four weeks earlier. Which constraint gives?

Time just shrank. To hold the launch you must either cut scope (fewer body options, defer a feature), add cost (overtime, expedited tooling, a second supplier), or accept lower quality (less testing) — and that last one is how projects like Orion Tech’s die. The PM’s job is to make that trade explicit and get a decision, not to quietly absorb it.

2.5 The five process phases

phase_x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)

  geom_line(color = "#2E86C1", linewidth = 1.1) +

           y = 0, yend = 1.05, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey55") +
  annotate("text", x = c(1, 3, 6, 8.6, 9.7), y = 1.12,
           label = c("Initiating", "Planning", "Executing", "Controlling", "Closing"),
           size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.2)) +
  labs(title = "Project management process life cycle",
       x = "Project timeline", y = "Resources and effort") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 2.2: Effort and resource use across the project life cycle. Little happens during initiation, effort peaks through execution and control, and it falls away at closing.












Phase
Key work




1. Initiating
Business case, feasibility, project sponsors, project charter + sign-off.


2. Planning
Scope statement, WBS, network diagram (AON), budget, risk plan, quality standards, control system, communication protocols. This phase decides success or failure.


3. Executing
Execute the plan, monitor progress, quality assurance. The PM shifts from doing to leading.


4. Controlling
Scope/change/schedule/budget/risk control become daily; overlaps execution.


5. Closing
Final review of budget, schedule, scope; customer sign-off; lessons learned; release resources; final payments. The hardest phase to finish well.




2.5.1 The project manager’s decision hierarchy
When decisions conflict, this is the order of consideration:

Safety (always first)
What is best for the company I represent
What is best for the project sponsor
What is best for the customer
What is best for the suppliers

And the PMI Code of Ethics rests on four pillars: responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty. You can violate ethics without breaking a law — but as an accredited PM you would swear to uphold the code, and breaking it puts your professional standing at risk.

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management and Communication
text:
2.6 Project communications
Communication is not a side task. About 90 % of a project manager’s time is spent communicating. The three communication processes are plan, manage, and control.

2.6.1 The communication plan
A written communication plan is built from the stakeholders’ information needs. Typical elements:

What information is collected, and when
Who receives it
How it is gathered and stored
Limits, if any, on who may tell whom
Reporting relationships
Contact information for all stakeholders
The distribution schedule for each type of communication



Orion Tech fix: what should have been in the plan on day one?

A stakeholder list with each party’s information needs; the report types (status, cost, risk, performance) and their frequency; the mix of channels (email for the record, chat for quick updates, dashboards for tracking, video for collaboration); and feedback loops so every team member confirms they understood the requirements. None of that existed — so requirements were guessed at and stakeholders were left in the dark.



2.6.2 The communication model
Every communication has three elements: a sender, a message, and a receiver. The sender encodes the message based on the receiver’s education, experience, language, and culture, picks the right method, and confirms it was understood. The receiver decodes carefully and checks their understanding. Feedback (“Does that make sense?”, a nod, a clarifying question) closes the loop.


2.6.3 Communication channels grow faster than the team
Add one person to a team and you do not add one relationship — you add one for every person already there. The number of two-way channels on a team of \(n\) people is:
\[\text{channels} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\]

n <- 2:15
ch <- n * (n - 1) / 2
df <- data.frame(n, ch)

ggplot(df, aes(n, ch)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5DADE2", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ch), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n) +
  labs(title = "Communication channels = n(n - 1) / 2",
       x = "People on the team (n)", y = "Two-way channels") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 2.3: Two-way communication channels versus team size. Doubling the team roughly quadruples the channels that have to be kept coherent.







2.6.4 Worked Example 1: channels on the RC-vehicle project
The core project has the PM, 4 team members, an accountant, and a sponsor liaison — 7 people. The extended stakeholder circle adds 2 supplier contacts, a retailer contact, and a compliance officer — 11 people.

core <- 7
extended <- 11

ch_core     <- core * (core - 1) / 2
ch_extended <- extended * (extended - 1) / 2

cat("Core team channels     :", ch_core, "\n")
cat("Extended circle channels:", ch_extended, "\n")
cat("Added by widening the circle from 7 to 11:", ch_extended - ch_core, "\n")

Core team channels     : 21 
Extended circle channels: 55 
Added by widening the circle from 7 to 11: 34 


Four extra people did not add four conversations — they added 34. That is the argument for a hub-and-spoke communication plan (routes defined, the PM as the hub) instead of letting everyone talk to everyone about everything.

section: 2.7 Listening: the mode we use most and understand least
text:
2.7 Listening: the mode we use most and understand least
The four modes of communication, by share of a typical day and by how well they are scientifically understood:



Mode
Share
Notes




Listening
~55 %
The most used, the least studied and taught


Speaking
~23 %



Reading
~13 %



Writing
~9 %




And most of the meaning is nonverbal: roughly 93 % of person-to-person communication is carried by body language (~55 %) and tone of voice (~38 %) — and tone’s share rises toward 86 % on the phone, where body language is gone.

Active listening: the receiver signals engagement — agreeing, asking for clarification.
Effective listening: watching the speaker for gesture and expression, thinking before responding, asking questions, repeating back, giving feedback.


2.7.1 The listening filters
Every message passes through three filters before it lands:

Selective attention — we choose what to focus on.
Selective interpretation — we impose our own meaning (shaped by gender, generation, geography, culture, education, occupation).
Selective retention — we choose what to keep, and for how long.

There is also a raw arithmetic problem. People listen at about 500 words per minute but speak at about 150. That leaves ~350 words per minute of spare capacity — room to tune out.


2.7.2 Try it yourself: the tune-out budget

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Listening de-railers — which one is Orion Tech’s problem?


Listening without focus — mind multitasking.
Listening without respect (impatience) — deciding the other person is wrong and interrupting.
Listening without respect (ego) — hearing only from your own perspective, not theirs.
Listening with bias (defensive / adverse) — building your rebuttal while they talk, or listening only for points to attack.

On Orion Tech it was mostly the first and last: dominant voices building responses instead of listening, quieter voices tuned out, and cross-cultural tone read through the listener’s own filter rather than the speaker’s intent.

2.8 Choosing a communication method









Written
Verbal




Formal
Complex problems, project plans, charters, long-distance — formal written
Presentations and speeches — formal verbal


Informal
Memos, emails (careful: email is also a contract), texts, notes — informal written

title: 2  Introduction to Project Management and Communication
text:
2.10 Key Takeaways

A project is temporary and unique; a process is permanent and repetitive. Only ~26 % of projects hit the full triple constraint — which is why the discipline exists.
The triple constraint is scope–time–cost, enclosing quality. Move one side and another must move, or quality pays.
Five phases: initiating, planning, executing, controlling, closing. Planning decides the outcome; closing is the hardest to finish.
Decisions are weighed safety → company → sponsor → customer → suppliers; ethics rest on responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty.
~90 % of a PM’s time is communication. Build a written communication plan from stakeholder needs, and close every loop with feedback.
Channels grow as \(n(n-1)/2\) — faster than headcount. Plan routes; don’t let everyone talk to everyone.
Listening is ~55 % of communication and the least trained; ~93 % of meaning is nonverbal. Watch for the selective attention/interpretation/retention filters and the de-railers.
Match the method (formal/informal × written/verbal) to the message, and the report (status/progress/trend/forecast/variance/EVM) to the stakeholder’s question.

text:
2.11 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Channel count and a reorganization

The RC-vehicle project currently routes all communication through a 6-person core team. A proposal would merge in 3 supplier engineers as full team members.

How many channels before and after?
By what percentage do channels increase versus the 50 % increase in headcount?

Solution.

before <- 6; after <- 9
ch <- function(n) n * (n - 1) / 2
cat("Before:", ch(before), "channels\n")
cat("After :", ch(after), "channels\n")
cat(sprintf("Headcount up %.0f%%, channels up %.0f%%\n",
            100 * (after / before - 1),
            100 * (ch(after) / ch(before) - 1)))

Before: 15 channels
After : 36 channels
Headcount up 50%, channels up 140%


Headcount rises 50 %, channels rise 125 %. Merging them in as full members triples the coordination load of those three people; a defined liaison route would add far less.



Problem 2: Pick the method (automotive, food, defense)

Choose formal/informal and written/verbal for each:

Notifying a defense customer that a delivered lot failed an acceptance test.
A daily 10-minute stand-up with the assembly team.
The project charter for the RC-vehicle launch.
Reminding a teammate that a drawing is due Friday.

Answers. 1 — formal written (contractual weight, complex, long-distance). 2 — informal verbal (meeting). 3 — formal written (plan/charter). 4 — informal written (a text or short email; keep a light record).



Problem 3 (discussion): rebuild Orion Tech’s communication system

If you were the PM, redesign the tools, reporting, and meetings to prevent the failure.
Model answer. Write a communication plan before launch. Use a mix: email for records, Teams/Slack for quick updates, dashboards for visual tracking, video calls for collaboration (so tone and context survive the offshore gap). Run regular status meetings with an agenda and action items, and have offshore developers present their own weekly updates so no group dominates. Send stakeholders a weekly progress report (status, cost, risk). Build feedback loops: every developer confirms, in their own words, what a requirement means before coding it. Use plain language, avoid idioms, and summarize decisions in writing.

3.2 Introduction: nothing official without a charter
Your company must get Senior Management to approve the Scope and Charter before work begins on the RC-vehicle replica. That is not bureaucracy — it is the difference between a project and a hobby. “There is no official project without an approved Project Charter.”
Two questions come first: should we do this project at all (selection), and exactly what are we committing to (scope). Then the organization’s shape — functional, projectized, or matrix — decides how much authority you actually have to deliver it.






Note



Industry snapshot. In automotive new-product introduction, a project cannot pass its first gate without a signed charter and a business case showing positive NPV. A food company scoping a new line writes a statement of work that names the throughput, the allergen controls, and what is explicitly out. A defense contractor’s SOW is a contract exhibit — every deliverable and exclusion in it is legally enforceable.

section: 3.3 Project selection: is it worth doing?
text:
3.3 Project selection: is it worth doing?

3.3.1 Payback period
The simplest screen: how long until the project’s net cash inflows repay the initial outlay?
\[\text{Payback} = \text{years until cumulative cash flow} \ge 0\]


3.3.2 Worked Example 1: payback on the RC-vehicle tooling investment
The project needs $450 000 up front (tooling, setup, approvals). Once the 100 000-unit contract runs, it returns an estimated $180 000 of net cash per year.

initial   <- 450000
annual_cf <- 180000
horizon   <- 5

cum <- cumsum(rep(annual_cf, horizon)) - initial
year_paid <- which(cum >= 0)[1]
# Fractional year within the payback year:
prev <- if (year_paid == 1) -initial else cum[year_paid - 1]
frac <- -prev / annual_cf

cat("Cumulative cash flow by year:", paste0("$", format(cum, big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat(sprintf("Payback period: %.2f years\n", (year_paid - 1) + frac))

Cumulative cash flow by year: $-270 000 $ -90 000 $  90 000 $ 270 000 $ 450 000 
Payback period: 2.50 years


Payback is quick to compute but ignores the time value of money and anything that happens after the payback point. NPV fixes both.


3.3.3 Net present value
NPV discounts every future cash flow back to today’s dollars at the organization’s required rate of return \(r\), then subtracts the initial outlay. A positive NPV means the project earns more than that hurdle rate.
\[NPV = -C_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1 + r)^t}\]


3.3.4 Try it yourself: NPV of the project

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


What happens to NPV if the hurdle rate rises to 18 %?

Raise r in the cell and re-run. Higher discount rates punish cash flows that arrive later, so NPV falls — a project that clears a 12 % hurdle may fail an 18 % one. This is why a company with expensive capital (or a risky project that demands a risk premium) is choosier about which projects it starts. Course Learning Outcome 1 is exactly this: communicate the philosophy of project selection using the NPV method.

text:
3.4 The project charter

PMI: developing a document that formally authorizes a project and documents the initial requirements that satisfy the stakeholders’ needs and expectations. Approval of the charter formally initiates the project.


3.4.1 Five inputs to a charter

Project Statement of Work — the high-level “project brief”: business need and product scope, fewer details than the scope statement.
Business Case — why the project is being done (the NPV/payback story).
Contract (if the client is external).
Enterprise Environmental Factors (EEFs) — conditions you cannot control (market, regulation, weather).
Organizational Process Assets (OPAs) — the company’s plans, processes, policies, and accumulated knowledge.



3.4.2 What a charter contains
Title and description; business case; pre-assigned resources; stakeholders and their known requirements; product deliverables and the end result; measurable objectives tied to strategy; a summary milestone schedule; a summary budget (gross only — the real budget comes after planning); approval requirements and who signs off; high-level risks; and signatures.


3.4.3 Why bother

Stakeholders are clearly defined
Communication channels are defined
Roles and responsibilities are outlined
Scope is defined — helping prevent scope creep
Better project processes in later phases
Higher probability of success
Buy-in from the team

The charter is a living document: update it as the project moves. Used well, it is “the single most important tool the project manager uses to manage the expectations of the sponsor and all other stakeholders.”

3.5 Stakeholders
A stakeholder is any individual or group with an active interest in the project who can affect it.







Internal
External




Senior management, accountant, team members, IT department
Client, competitors, suppliers, environmental agencies, government agencies, research labs



Managing them is a loop: identify → gather information → determine strengths and weaknesses → predict behaviour → build an engagement strategy → implement. The point of engagement is to increase support and reduce resistance — by listening, informing, and helping stakeholders along.

text:
3.6 The scope statement
Written early in planning, the scope statement is more detailed than the charter and should include:

The project statement (what will be done)
Acceptance criteria and the validation/testing plan
Deliverables
Exclusions (what is explicitly not in scope)
Constraints and assumptions
Project coordination
Signed-off review with the customer and with corporate management

Product scope = the features and functions of the thing you are building. Project scope = the work needed to deliver it. A scope statement covers both, plus boundaries and references to specs. As the project progresses, scope should get clearer and more specific — and changes here should be avoided, though not forbidden.

3.6.1 The scope management processes
Plan scope → collect requirements → define scope → create WBS → validate scope (at closing) → control scope (throughout). The scope management plan is often run as an extension of Management by Objectives (MBO): set unambiguous, realistic objectives; check periodically whether they are being met; take corrective action.

title: 3  Project Scope, Charter, and Organizational Structures
text:
3.7 Scope creep
Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of requirements over the project’s life:

one deliverable quietly becomes five
three “essential” features become ten
mid-project, the customer’s needs change and requirements are reopened

Its usual causes are stakeholders changing requirements and internal miscommunication. It is not always bad — customer needs genuinely evolve, and refusing all change can deliver the wrong product. The problem is uncontrolled change. A good PM expects it and plans for it with a change-control process: every change request is logged, its impact on scope, schedule, and cost is assessed, and it is approved or rejected before work changes.

3.8 Organizational culture
Every organization develops its own outlook, policies, habits of thought, and norms — “as unique as a fingerprint.” Culture is the solution to problems that has worked consistently for a group and is therefore taught to new members as the correct way to perceive and think. It is shaped by technology, environment, geographic location, reward systems, rules and procedures, key organizational members, and critical incidents.
Culture affects projects through:

Department interaction — cooperative cultures run projects far better than adversarial ones.
Employee commitment to goals — teams need to understand the why to be motivated.
Project planning — some cultures tolerate padding estimates but not being late.
Performance evaluation — a culture that rewards innovation breeds aggressive, high-payoff project management (with occasional big losses).

3.9 Organizational structures
How the lines of authority and communication are arranged decides when people are available and how you get them.

  )







Figure 3.2: Project manager authority across organizational structures. It rises from almost none in a functional organization to near-total in a projectized one, with the matrix band in between.













Structure
Strengths for the PM
Weaknesses for the PM




Functional (grouped by specialty; one clear boss; each department runs its own projects)
No restructuring needed; deep expertise; everyone knows their place
Many layers to reach people; weak customer focus; projects drag because staff have “day jobs” and other priorities


Projectized (the company just does projects; team co-located)
One reporting line; easy communication; fast decisions; strong PMs; rapid market response
Teams are expensive to set up and maintain; loyalty to the project over the organization; hard to keep a shared pool of expertise; team anxiety about “what next” when the project ends


Matrix (blend; classified weak / balanced / strong by PM influence)
Suited to dynamic environments; values both project and functional efficiency; coordinates across units; maximizes scarce shared resources
Two bosses; heavy time spent negotiating shared resources; frustrating for staff caught between project and functional demands





Which structure is the RC-vehicle project running in?

Almost certainly a matrix — the company has an existing manufacturing line and functional departments (design, quality, purchasing), and it borrows people into the project. That means the PM shares the design engineers with their functional manager and must negotiate their time. Expect the “administrative conflict” of Chapter 10: every matrix team member has two bosses.

title: 3  Project Scope, Charter, and Organizational Structures
text:
3.10 Key Takeaways

Select projects on merit: payback is quick but ignores the time value of money; NPV discounts every future cash flow and is the course’s standard (CLO 1). Positive NPV = beats the hurdle rate.
The charter formally initiates the project. Inputs: SOW, business case, contract, EEFs, OPAs. It defines stakeholders, roles, and scope, and earns team buy-in. No approved charter, no official project.
Manage stakeholders on a power–interest grid: manage the high-power/high-interest closely, monitor the rest.
The scope statement covers product and project scope, plus acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints, and assumptions, and is signed off.
Scope creep is uncontrolled requirement growth. Change is normal; uncontrolled change is the enemy — run every request through change control for a cost/schedule impact and a decision.
Culture shapes project outcomes through department cooperation, commitment, planning honesty, and what performance evaluation rewards.
Structure sets the PM’s real authority: near zero in functional, near total in projectized, negotiated in the matrix (weak/balanced/strong) — where everyone has two bosses.

text:
3.11 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Payback vs. NPV disagree

Project A: $300 000 outlay, then $150 000/yr for 3 years, nothing after. Project B: $300 000 outlay, then $90 000/yr for 6 years. Hurdle rate 10 %. Which has the shorter payback, and which has the higher NPV?
Solution.

npv <- function(c0, cfs, r) -c0 + sum(cfs / (1 + r)^seq_along(cfs))
A <- c(150000, 150000, 150000)
B <- rep(90000, 6)
cat(sprintf("A: payback 2.0 yr, NPV $%s\n", format(round(npv(3e5, A, 0.10)), big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("B: payback ~3.3 yr, NPV $%s\n", format(round(npv(3e5, B, 0.10)), big.mark = " ")))

A: payback 2.0 yr, NPV $73 028
B: payback ~3.3 yr, NPV $91 973


A pays back faster; B has the higher NPV because its cash flows keep coming for three more years. Payback alone would pick the worse project.



Problem 2: Charter or scope statement?

Which document does each belong in?

“Gross budget: approximately $650 000.” → Charter (summary budget).
“Body colourways: Racing Red and Gunmetal only; no custom colours.” → Scope statement (exclusions).
“Sponsor: VP Operations. Signs off at Gate 1.” → Charter (approval/signatures).
“Drop test: survives 10 drops from 1.5 m onto concrete, no functional damage.” → Scope statement (acceptance criteria).




Problem 3 (discussion): the functional manager won’t release the good engineer

In a weak matrix, your best-choice design engineer’s functional manager keeps assigning them to department work and offers you a junior instead. Using the culture and structure ideas in this chapter, explain why this happens and what you can do.
Discussion points. The functional manager is evaluated on their department’s output, so they hoard their strongest people — a reward-system effect. In a weak matrix you have little formal authority to override it. Levers: escalate to the sponsor (whose NPV depends on the project), negotiate a part-time or time-boxed assignment, trade a deliverable the functional manager cares about, or get the resource commitment written into the charter so it is a documented agreement rather than a favour.

text:
4.2 Introduction: the project manager as mini-CEO
Leading the RC-vehicle project means more than tracking a Gantt chart. The brief has your team learning a new assembly line with a real learning curve, working with an unproven supplier, and racing a holiday deadline. The PM “encapsulates the role of a mini-CEO” — expected to manage holistically from start to finish: acquiring resources, motivating and building the team, holding a vision and fighting fires, and communicating relentlessly. “A PM cannot get up in the morning and think ‘I don’t want to communicate today.’”






Note



Industry snapshot. On an automotive launch, the line lead who can only give orders stalls the moment a novel problem appears; the one who has built a team that raises issues early hits the job-one date. In food processing, a sanitation crew that understands why the changeover procedure matters follows it at 3 a.m. when no one is watching. Leadership is what fills the gap between the procedure and reality.

title: 4  Leadership and the Project Manager
text:
4.3 Leadership versus management
Leadership is the ability to inspire confidence and support among the people needed to achieve organizational goals. A manager holds a title that lets them plan, organize, direct, and control others. Leadership may be part of the manager’s job, but the other roles are more administrative.
Leaders create a sense of partnership. Four things build it:







Foundation
What it means




Exchange of purpose
Every member knows the project’s goals and vision.


A right to say “no”
Members can voice professional disagreement. Losing an argument is acceptable; losing the right to disagree is not.


Joint accountability
Every member owns the project’s outcomes — good or bad.


Absolute honesty
All information becomes community information.




lm <- data.frame(
  aspect = c("Focus", "Asks", "Relies on", "Time horizon",
             "Handles change by", "Success is"),
  manager = c("Systems & structure", "How & when", "Control", "Short term",
              "Administering", "Doing things right"),
  leader  = c("People", "What & why", "Trust", "Longer term",
              "Setting direction", "Doing the right things")
)
lm_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(lm, c(manager, leader),
                               names_to = "role", values_to = "text")
lm_long$aspect <- factor(lm_long$aspect, levels = rev(lm$aspect))
lm_long$role <- factor(lm_long$role, levels = c("manager", "leader"),
                       labels = c("MANAGER", "LEADER"))

ggplot(lm_long, aes(role, aspect)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = role), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = text), size = 3.1 * diagram_text_scale, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("MANAGER" = "#AED6F1", "LEADER" = "#A9DFBF"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Two hats the project manager wears", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 4.1: Manager and leader emphases. Neither column is ‘bad’ — a project manager needs both, but leans on the right-hand behaviours during execution.






4.3.1 Bennis’s four competencies of the new project leader

The power of appreciation — recognize and reward others’ talent; your job is not to outshine the team but to let it develop.
Keep reminding people what’s important — amid the noise of problems, keep everyone’s eye on the prize.
Generate and sustain trust — through authenticity, fairness, honesty, and caring. Honesty is the trait people look for most.
The leader and the led are intimate allies — leadership supports the team’s effort; it does not dominate it.

title: 4  Leadership and the Project Manager
text:
4.4 The five leadership styles
Effective PMs switch styles to fit the person and the situation.








Style
Use it when
The downside if overused




Command & control
You know the best way and the other person doesn’t; beginners; a crisis
Team feels devalued; learned helplessness; kills creativity and initiative


Relating
Building rapport, bonding the team, focusing people on common goals
Can’t make tough calls or take charge in a crisis; seen as weak


Democratic
Planning — getting buy-in and reality-based plans from those who will execute
Execution often needs autocracy; consensus-building wastes a critical deadline


Hands-on
You must step in and model the way to get a stuck task done
Disempowering; low morale; you become the bottleneck


Coaching
Long-term development; asking questions that lead people to their own solutions
Slow for short-term objectives — but it is the style most managers most need to build

4.5 Building the team
Teams develop through predictable stages, and the leader’s job changes with each:

stage_x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
perf <- 0.4 + 0.15 * sin(stage_x) +
        pmin(0.5, 0.06 * stage_x) -
        0.22 * exp(-((stage_x - 2.2)^2) / 0.6)
df <- data.frame(x = stage_x, perf = pmin(pmax(perf, 0.1), 1))

ggplot(df, aes(x, perf)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E86C1", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1, 2.4, 4.6, 7.2, 9.4), y = 1.03,
           label = c("Forming", "Storming", "Norming", "Performing", "Adjourning"),
           fontface = "bold", size = 3.1 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1.7, 3.5, 6, 8.6), xend = c(1.7, 3.5, 6, 8.6),
           y = 0.1, yend = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey60") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.1, 1.1)) +
  labs(title = "Tuckman's stages of team development",
       x = "Time together", y = "Team performance") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 4.3: Team performance through Tuckman’s stages. Performance dips during storming before rising; a leader who expects the dip manages it instead of panicking.






Forming — polite, uncertain. Leader: direct — clarify goals, roles, the charter.
Storming — conflict over approach and authority; performance dips. Leader: coach — surface conflict, don’t suppress it.
Norming — norms settle, trust builds. Leader: support.
Performing — the team runs itself. Leader: delegate.
Adjourning — the project ends; recognize contributions and manage the transition (see Chapter 13).

text:
4.6 Motivating the team

4.6.1 Worked Example 1: Herzberg — is this a hygiene problem or a motivator problem?
Herzberg splits job factors into hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policy, supervision — their absence causes dissatisfaction, but their presence does not motivate) and motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth — these drive engagement).

complaints <- data.frame(
  issue = c("Cramped, hot project room", "No recognition for hitting the drop-test milestone",
            "Confusing expense policy", "Same repetitive CAD cleanup every week",
            "Parking is far from the building"),
  type = c("Hygiene", "Motivator", "Hygiene", "Motivator", "Hygiene")
)
print(complaints, row.names = FALSE)

fix_first <- complaints$issue[complaints$type == "Hygiene"]
cat("\nFix the hygiene issues to stop dissatisfaction:\n - ",
    paste(fix_first, collapse = "\n - "), "\n", sep = "")
cat("\nThen add motivators (recognition, varied/owned work) to actually raise engagement.\n")

                                              issue      type
                          Cramped, hot project room   Hygiene
 No recognition for hitting the drop-test milestone Motivator
                           Confusing expense policy   Hygiene
             Same repetitive CAD cleanup every week Motivator
                   Parking is far from the building   Hygiene

Fix the hygiene issues to stop dissatisfaction:
 - Cramped, hot project room
 - Confusing expense policy
 - Parking is far from the building

Then add motivators (recognition, varied/owned work) to actually raise engagement.




4.6.2 Try it yourself: expectancy theory
Vroom’s expectancy model says motivation is the product of three beliefs, each 0–1: Expectancy (effort → performance), Instrumentality (performance → reward), and Valence (how much the person wants the reward).
\[\text{Motivation} = E \times I \times V\]
Because it is a product, any factor near zero kills motivation.

text:
4.7 Emotional intelligence
Goleman: the most effective leaders all have a high degree of emotional intelligence — IQ and technical skill are just the entry ticket. Five components:

Self-awareness — a clear view of your strengths, weaknesses, drives, and ego needs.
Self-regulation — keeping yourself under control; think before you act.
Motivation — driven to your own potential and to drawing the best from each team member.
Empathy — weighing team members’ feelings when making a decision.
Social skill — managing relationships with purpose.

title: 4  Leadership and the Project Manager
text:
4.8 Key Takeaways

Management administers systems; leadership inspires people. A PM needs both and leans on leadership during execution.
Partnership rests on exchange of purpose, the right to say no, joint accountability, and absolute honesty. Bennis: appreciate, remind what matters, build trust, be an ally.
Switch among the five styles — command & control, relating, democratic, hands-on, coaching — by situation. Plan democratically; often execute autocratically. Every style overused has a cost.
Teams move through forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning; performance dips in storming — expect it and coach through it.
Diagnose motivation with Herzberg (fix hygiene to stop dissatisfaction, add motivators to raise engagement) and expectancy (\(E \times I \times V\) — any factor near zero kills it).
Emotional intelligence — self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skill — separates effective project leaders from merely competent ones.

title: 4  Leadership and the Project Manager
text:
4.9 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Pick the style

Which leadership style fits each moment on the RC-vehicle project?

Kicking off planning for the WBS with the whole team. → Democratic (buy-in, reality-based plan).
A moulding press fails at 2 a.m. and the launch date is at risk. → Command & control (crisis; take charge).
A capable senior designer is bored and thinking of leaving. → Coaching (long-term development; varied, owned work).
A brand-new co-op student has never used the company’s PLM system. → Command & control initially, moving to coaching.
The team has gelled and is hitting milestones on its own. → Delegating / supporting — stay out of the way.




Problem 2: Expectancy diagnosis

A skilled technician has stopped putting in effort on validation testing. In a one-on-one you learn they are certain the extra effort won’t change the delivery date because “purchasing will be late anyway.” Which expectancy factor is broken, and what do you do?
Answer. Instrumentality — they no longer believe performance leads to the outcome. Restoring it means making the link visible again: show how the test results actually gate the next milestone, remove the purchasing blocker or re-sequence around it, and close the loop when their work does move the date.



Problem 3 (discussion): the hands-on trap

You are the strongest CAD modeller on the team, and every time someone struggles you take the model over and finish it yourself. The work gets done and is high-quality. Why is this a leadership failure, and what should you do instead?
Discussion points. Taking over is the hands-on style overused: it is disempowering, tanks morale, stops people learning, and makes you the bottleneck — the project’s throughput is now capped by your personal hours. The coaching move is to ask questions that lead the person to the fix, sit with them while they do it, and follow up — slower once, faster forever.

Before we begin: how do you eat an elephant?

One bite at a time. “Project managers cannot manage projects. Project managers manage pieces of projects.” The WBS is how you cut the elephant into bites.

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
section: 5.2 Introduction: from a scope statement to something you can manage
text:
5.2 Introduction: from a scope statement to something you can manage
You have a signed scope statement for the RC-vehicle replica. It is still far too big to schedule, budget, or assign. The work breakdown structure is the bridge: it takes the total scope and breaks it into deliverables, then work packages, then activities small enough that one person can own each one and you can put a real number on it.

Definition. A WBS is a deliverable-oriented grouping of project components that organizes and defines the total scope of the project.

A well-built WBS lets the team plan every step, collect and organize the information each task needs, and assign manageable chunks to team members. It also enables the WBS dictionary, which pins down the requirements for each task.






Note



Industry snapshot. An automotive program WBS separates body, powertrain integration, electrical, validation, and launch — each a deliverable, not an action. A food-plant install WBS breaks out utilities, process equipment, controls, sanitation qualification, and commissioning. A defense contract WBS follows a mandated standard (MIL-STD-881) so the customer can track cost against the exact same structure the contractor uses.

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.4 Design principles

5.4.1 The 100 % rule
The WBS includes 100 % of the work in the scope — all deliverables, internal, external, and interim — and no more. At every level, the sum of the children equals the parent, and nothing outside the scope appears.


5.4.2 Worked Example 1: does this WBS roll up to 100 %?
The “1.1 Body & Frame” deliverable is estimated at 340 hours. Its four work packages are estimated at 120, 90, 70, and 60 hours.

parent_hours   <- 340
children_hours <- c("1.1.1 Outer body design" = 120,
                    "1.1.2 Inner frame design" = 90,
                    "1.1.3 Material selection" = 70,
                    "1.1.4 Design review & release" = 60)

child_sum <- sum(children_hours)
cat("Children:\n"); print(children_hours)
cat(sprintf("\nSum of children : %d h\n", child_sum))
cat(sprintf("Parent estimate : %d h\n", parent_hours))

if (child_sum == parent_hours) {
  cat("OK - the children account for exactly 100% of the parent.\n")
} else if (child_sum < parent_hours) {
  cat(sprintf("GAP - %d h of the parent's scope is not captured by any work package.\n",
              parent_hours - child_sum))
} else {
  cat(sprintf("OVER - the children exceed the parent by %d h (>100%% -- scope crept in).\n",
              child_sum - parent_hours))
}

Children:
      1.1.1 Outer body design      1.1.2 Inner frame design 
                          120                            90 
     1.1.3 Material selection 1.1.4 Design review & release 
                           70                            60 

Sum of children : 340 h
Parent estimate : 340 h
OK - the children account for exactly 100% of the parent.


Here the children sum to 340 — the deliverable is fully decomposed with nothing missing and nothing extra.


5.4.3 Mutually exclusive
No overlap between WBS elements. Overlap causes duplicated work, confusion over who is responsible, and messy cost accounting. If element names are ambiguous, the WBS dictionary disambiguates them.


5.4.4 Plan outcomes, not actions
Define elements as results (“Training module completed”), not actions (“write script”, “record video”, “upload”). Action lists always capture too many or too few steps — breaking the 100 % rule — and they over-prescribe how the work is done, killing the team’s ingenuity.

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.5 Level of detail
A work package at the activity level is a task that:

can be realistically and confidently estimated;
makes no practical sense to break down further;
produces a measurable deliverable; and
forms a unique package that could be outsourced or contracted out.

Rules of thumb for how far to decompose:

80-hour rule — no work package (single deliverable at the lowest level) exceeds ~80 hours of effort.
One reporting period — no package is longer than a single progress-reporting period (if you report monthly, nothing runs longer than a month).
8-hour floor — generally do not define a task below ~8 hours; below that you are micromanaging.
“If it makes sense” — apply common sense.

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.7 The WBS dictionary
The dictionary is used to control what work is done and when, prevent scope creep, and capture the effort for each task. Physically, teams post the work packages on a wall in logical work-flow order; removing them in numerical order generates the dictionary. Each entry — a task description — records:

Task description (what work is authorized)
Quantified objectives and deliverables (cross-referenced to the charter)
Product description; acceptance criteria (how the owner checks their own work)
Assumptions; resources assigned; duration; cost; due date
Interdependencies (before this task / after this task)
Project manager approval and date

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.8 Work authorization and contracts
Once the scope is decomposed into work packages, stakeholders formally agree on project content — the work authorization. If the client is external, this includes the contract sign-off.
A valid project-management contract requires all six of:

The legal right to contract
Legal age (18 in Ontario and Quebec; 19 or 21 elsewhere in Canada)
Sound mind at signing
Valid, legal consideration for both parties
A legal scope of work
Offer and acceptance

Contracts also commonly contain: excusable delays; allowable costs; liquidated damages (non-performance / penalty clauses); inspection criteria; responsibility for correcting defects; and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
