title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.9 Key Takeaways

A WBS is a deliverable-oriented decomposition of the total scope into deliverables → work packages → activities. PMs manage the pieces.
Numbering encodes the hierarchy: Level 1 project, Level 2 deliverables, Level 3+ work packages.
Obey the three design rules: 100 % rule (children sum to the parent, never more), mutually exclusive (no overlap), and plan outcomes, not actions.
Size work packages with the 8/80 rule and the one-reporting-period rule; below ~8 h you are micromanaging, above ~80 h you cannot estimate confidently.
The WBS feeds estimating, scheduling, staffing, and risk — errors propagate to all four.
The WBS dictionary locks down each task’s description, acceptance criteria, resources, and interdependencies, and helps prevent scope creep.
Work authorization formalizes agreement on content; a valid contract needs all six legal elements and usually carries liquidated-damages and dispute clauses.

title: 5  Work Breakdown Structures (WBS)
text:
5.10 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Fix the 100 % rule violation

The “1.3 Assembly & Test” deliverable is estimated at 300 h. Its packages are listed as: Prototype assembly (110 h), Drop test (60 h), EMC test (70 h), Prototype assembly rework (40 h), Write the test report (30 h), and “General project management (50 h).”
What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
Solution. The children sum to 360 h — 60 h over 100 % of the parent. Two problems: “Prototype assembly rework” overlaps “Prototype assembly” (not mutually exclusive — fold rework into the assembly package or make it a contingency), and “General project management” is not part of this deliverable’s scope — PM effort belongs in its own Level-2 element (e.g. “1.0.1 Project Management”), not smuggled into a technical deliverable.



Problem 2: Outcome or action?

Rewrite these action-style entries as outcome-style WBS elements:

“Call three carbon-fibre suppliers and get quotes”
“Run the mould 20 times and measure the parts”
“Email the drawings to the customer for approval”

Model answers. 1 → “Carbon-fibre supplier selected and quoted.” 2 → “Moulding process capability established.” 3 → “Customer design approval obtained.” Each is a result you can mark done or not done, and it does not dictate the method.



Problem 3 (discussion): how deep should the RC-vehicle WBS go?

Your draft WBS has a work package “Design the outer body” estimated at 180 h and spanning 6 weeks, and another, “Deburr the frame jig”, estimated at 2 h. Using the rules of thumb, what do you do with each?
Discussion points. “Design the outer body” breaks both the 80-hour rule and (if you report every 2 weeks) the single-reporting-period rule — split it into concept, detailed CAD, and design-release packages. “Deburr the frame jig” is below the 8-hour floor — roll it into the jig-fabrication package rather than tracking it as its own line.

text:
6.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
Build an activity-on-node (AON) network from a precedence table.
Apply the rules for constructing a valid network diagram.
Perform the forward pass to find early start (ES) and early finish (EF).
Perform the backward pass to find late start (LS) and late finish (LF).
Calculate total float and identify the critical path.
Compute a three-point (PERT) activity duration.
Choose a strategy to shorten the critical path when the project is too long.



Before we begin: which task can slip without moving the deadline?

On any project some tasks have slack and some do not. Guessing wrong — pouring effort into a task with float while a zero-float task quietly slips — is one of the most common ways schedules die. The network diagram tells you which is which.

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.2 Introduction: when can we launch?
The RC-vehicle WBS gives you a list of activities and their durations. It does not tell you how long the whole project takes, because the activities are not all independent — you cannot assemble a prototype before the body is designed. A network diagram captures those dependencies and answers the question the sponsor actually cares about: what is the earliest the project can finish, and which activities decide that date?






Note



Industry snapshot. Every automotive program plan is a critical-path network: the “job one” date is the length of the longest dependent chain. A food-plant commissioning schedule uses the same math to decide whether sanitation qualification can overlap controls checkout. A defense contractor reports critical-path status to the customer monthly — slipping a critical task is a contractual event.

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.3 From WBS to precedence table
For each activity you need its duration and its immediate predecessors — the activities that must finish before it can start. Rules for a valid AON network:

Determine precedence ordering before drawing.
Networks flow left to right.
An activity cannot begin until all connected predecessors are complete.
Arrows show precedence and logical flow (they may cross, but minimize it).
Every activity has a unique identifier.
No looping back to an earlier activity.
It is common (not required) to start from a single start node…
…and end at a single end node.

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)

Each activity is a box with six numbers:

6.5.1 Forward pass (ES, EF)
Move left to right. \(EF = ES + DUR\). Carry each EF forward as the successor’s ES — except at a merge, where the ES is the largest incoming EF.


6.5.2 Backward pass (LS, LF)
Move right to left from the project finish. \(LS = LF - DUR\). Carry each LS back as the predecessor’s LF — except at a burst, where the LF is the smallest outgoing LS.


6.5.3 Float and the critical path
\[FLT = LS - ES = LF - EF\]
Activities with zero float cannot slip without delaying the whole project — together they form the critical path.

# A small critical-path solver (base R + data.frame).
cpm <- function(df) {
  df$pred <- strsplit(df$pred, ",")
  n <- nrow(df); id <- df$id
  ES <- EF <- LS <- LF <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, n), id)

  # Forward pass (ids are already in a valid topological order here)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    p <- df$pred[[i]]; p <- p[p != ""]
    ES[i] <- if (length(p) == 0) 0 else max(EF[p])
    EF[i] <- ES[i] + df$dur[i]
  }
  proj <- max(EF)

  # Backward pass
  for (i in rev(seq_len(n))) {
    succ <- id[sapply(df$pred, function(pp) id[i] %in% pp)]
    LF[i] <- if (length(succ) == 0) proj else min(LS[succ])
    LS[i] <- LF[i] - df$dur[i]
  }

  data.frame(Activity = id, Dur = df$dur,
             ES = ES, EF = EF, LS = LS, LF = LF,
             Float = LS - ES,
             Critical = ifelse(LS - ES == 0, "  <- critical", ""))
}

res <- cpm(acts)
print(res, row.names = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("\nProject duration: %d days\n", max(res$EF)))
cat("Critical path:", paste(res$Activity[res$Float == 0], collapse = " - "), "\n")

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.6 Three-point (PERT) duration estimates
When a duration is uncertain, estimate three values — optimistic \(o\), most likely \(m\), pessimistic \(p\) — and combine them:
\[t_e = \frac{o + 4m + p}{6}\]

6.6.1 Try it yourself: PERT durations

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Why the weight of 4 on the most-likely value?

PERT assumes each activity duration follows a Beta distribution skewed toward the most-likely value, with the optimistic and pessimistic values as the tails. Weighting \(m\) by 4 and \(o\), \(p\) by 1 each (dividing by 6) is the standard approximation of that distribution’s mean. The activity standard deviation \((p - o)/6\) becomes important in Chapter 8, where you combine them to find the probability of finishing on time.

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.7 Shortening the critical path
Only work on the critical path shortens the project. Options, roughly in order of preference:

Eliminate critical tasks (is it truly needed?).
Re-plan series paths to run in parallel.
Overlap sequential tasks (start the successor before the predecessor fully finishes — fast-tracking).
Shorten durations on critical activities — prefer earlier-starting tasks, then the longest, then the easiest, then the ones cheapest to speed up.

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.8 The downside of network diagrams

Often not drawn to scale — time is just a number, which can create a false sense of how much time is available.
Can be too large and complex to be useful.
Faulty construction logic can oversimplify or misrepresent the work.
Sometimes used for work they do not suit.
Positive bias creeps into PERT estimates (people are optimistic).

title: 6  Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON)
text:
6.9 Key Takeaways

Build the AON network from a precedence table (durations + immediate predecessors); it flows left to right with no loops.
Forward pass: \(EF = ES + DUR\); at a merge, ES = the largest incoming EF. Gives the project duration.
Backward pass: \(LS = LF - DUR\); at a burst, LF = the smallest outgoing LS.
Float \(= LS - ES = LF - EF\). Zero-float activities form the critical path — the longest dependent chain, and the only one worth shortening.
PERT: \(t_e = (o + 4m + p)/6\), activity SD \(= (p - o)/6\).
Shorten the critical path by eliminating, parallelizing, overlapping, or crashing critical tasks — and re-check, because the critical path can shift.

Problem 2: PERT and the optimistic tail

An activity is estimated at \(o = 6\), \(m = 9\), \(p = 24\) days.

What is \(t_e\)? (b) Why is \(t_e\) noticeably larger than \(m\)? (c) What is the activity standard deviation?

Solution. (a) \(t_e = (6 + 36 + 24)/6 = 11\) days. (b) The pessimistic tail is far from the most-likely value (24 vs 9) while the optimistic tail is close (6 vs 9), so the distribution is right-skewed and its mean sits above \(m\). (c) SD \(= (24 - 6)/6 = 3\) days — a wide, risky activity.



Problem 3 (discussion): which task do you crash?

On the sub-project network, the critical path is A–B–C–E–G–I–J (38 days) and the sponsor needs 34. Crash data: B costs $500/day to shorten (max 3 days), G costs $1 200/day (max 2 days), E costs $300/day (max 2 days). Which combination gets you to 34 days at least cost, and what do you check afterward?
Discussion points. You need 4 days. Cheapest first: E for 2 days ($600), then B for 2 days ($1 000) — total $1 600 for 4 days. Avoid G at $1 200/day. Then re-run the network: after removing 4 days from this chain, another path (e.g. A–B–C–F–H–J) may now be critical or co-critical, and crashing further would have to shorten both.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
Distinguish risk from uncertainty, and threats from opportunities.
Classify a risk and write a well-formed risk statement.
Run a qualitative analysis with a probability–impact matrix.
Compute expected monetary value (EMV) and solve a simple decision tree.
Select a response strategy: accept, minimize, share, transfer, or reserve.
Size a contingency reserve and distinguish task contingency from managerial contingency.
Explain how FMEA supports project risk management.



Before we begin: name one thing that could sink the RC-vehicle project

Now: how likely is it, and how bad would it be? You just did qualitative risk analysis. The rest of this chapter makes it systematic.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.2 Introduction: the known unknowns
The RC-vehicle brief is a risk register waiting to be written. One candidate motor supplier is unproven and its staff are negotiating a first labour contract. The carbon-fibre supplier is mid-restructuring after a foreign acquisition. Choosing a new assembly line brings a learning curve. None of these is a certainty — but each is identifiable, and that is exactly what makes it a risk rather than an uncertainty.

Risk = the probability or threat of loss, injury, or any negative occurrence caused by internal or external vulnerabilities, that can be reduced by preemptive action.
An uncertainty is when neither the probability nor the mode of occurrence is known. If you do not know about it, you cannot act on it.

The core equation:
\[\text{Risk} = \text{Probability of event} \times \text{Impact of event}\]
Probability is usually a percentage; impact is dollars or schedule delay. Risk and opportunity are mirror images — an opportunity is an unforeseen event with a positive outcome, handled with the same tools for the opposite end.






Note



Industry snapshot. Aircraft makers such as Bombardier minimize part risk by forcing every significant supplier into direct contact with their quality department and auditing their processes. The European Space Agency and Airbus share the risk of a new airframe across nations because no one country can carry it. A fixed-price defense contract transfers budget-overrun risk to the vendor.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.3 The four-stage process

Risk identification — determine the specific risk factors that can reasonably be expected to affect the project.
Analysis of probability and consequences — how likely, and how bad.
Risk mitigation strategies — steps to reduce the impact of the risks judged threatening enough to act on.
Control and documentation — track the risks and build a knowledge base for future projects from the lessons learned.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.4 Risk identification and classification
Sort each identified risk into a class. A common (not exhaustive) list:

Financial — material price moves, currency, budget cuts
Technology — unproven design or process
Resources — key people, equipment availability
Schedule — dependency slips, long lead times
Weather, Political, Environmental

Techniques: structured brainstorming, interviewing to get optimistic / most-likely / pessimistic views of an event, probability distributions to represent uncertain outcomes, and expert judgment to validate.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.5 Qualitative analysis: the probability–impact matrix
Plot each risk by likelihood (x-axis) and impact (y-axis). The top-right is red (mitigation planned in advance), the middle band yellow (team decides whether to plan), the bottom-left green (just stay aware).

grid <- expand.grid(prob = 1:5, impact = 1:5)
grid$score <- grid$prob * grid$impact
grid$zone <- cut(grid$score, c(0, 6, 12, 25),
                 labels = c("Green", "Yellow", "Red"))

risks <- data.frame(
  risk = c("Unproven supplier can't deliver", "Carbon-fibre plant disruption",
           "New line learning curve overruns", "Labour action at supplier",
           "Steel price spike", "Minor drawing errors"),
  prob = c(3, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4),
  impact = c(5, 4, 3, 5, 2, 1)
)

ggplot(grid, aes(prob, impact)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = zone), color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Green = "#A9DFBF", Yellow = "#F9E79F", Red = "#F5B7B1"),
                    name = "Zone") +
  geom_point(data = risks, aes(prob, impact), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             size = 3, color = "#1B4F72") +
  geom_text(data = risks, aes(prob, impact, label = risk), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 2.7 * diagram_text_scale, vjust = -1, hjust = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = c("Very low", "Low", "Medium", "High", "Very high")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = c("Negligible", "Minor", "Moderate", "Major", "Severe")) +
  labs(title = "Probability x Impact", x = "Probability", y = "Impact") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9.5 * diagram_text_scale)
  )

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.6 Quantitative analysis
Tools: sensitivity analysis (which risks move the outcome most), expected monetary value (the probability-weighted average outcome), decision trees (lay out choices and chance events), and Monte Carlo simulation (run the network thousands of times with sampled durations/costs).

7.6.1 Worked Example 1: EMV of a single risk
The “new assembly line learning curve” risk: a 40 % chance it adds $120 000 of rework and overtime; otherwise $0.

p_occurs <- 0.40
impact   <- 120000

emv <- p_occurs * impact + (1 - p_occurs) * 0
cat(sprintf("EMV of this risk: 0.40 x $%s = $%s\n",
            format(impact, big.mark = " "), format(emv, big.mark = " ")))
cat("This is the amount you would budget in a risk reserve to 'cover' this one risk on average.\n")

EMV of this risk: 0.40 x $120 000 = $48 000
This is the amount you would budget in a risk reserve to 'cover' this one risk on average.




7.6.2 Try it yourself: decision tree — buy the copper now or later?
You need 750 lb of copper for the RC-vehicle wiring harness tooling. Buy it now and pay $100 storage, or buy it later at the summer price — which is $5.58/lb with 90 % probability, or $4.50/lb with 10 % probability.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


What would flip the decision?

Raise the probability of the low summer price, widen the price gap, or cut the storage cost toward zero and “buy later” wins by more. Push storage cost up (a bonded warehouse, insurance, spoilage) or make the high price nearly certain and “buy now” wins. A decision tree makes the tipping point explicit instead of leaving it to gut feel.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.7 Response strategies








Strategy
What it means
Example on our project




Accept
The risk is minor or unlikely enough to live with
Small drawing errors — caught in review, low cost


Minimize
Reduce probability or impact
Audit the unproven supplier; put their staff in contact with your quality team


Share
Split the risk (and reward) with a partner
Co-develop the new control system with the supplier under a shared-savings deal


Transfer
Shift the risk to another party
Fixed-price contract (vendor eats overruns); liquidated damages for non-performance


Contingency reserve
Set aside funds/time for the risk if it hits
10–15 % reserve against the carbon-fibre and learning-curve risks


Other
Anything else fit for the situation
Dual-source the motor; pre-qualify a backup



For opportunities, the mirror strategies are exploit, share, enhance, and accept.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.8 Contingency reserves
Two kinds:

Task (project) contingency — offsets overruns on individual tasks/work packages. Managed by the project manager. As work completes, reserve for finished tasks is released and cannot be reused.
Managerial contingency — a project-level buffer for scope changes forced by the customer, “acts of God,” and other unforeseeable events. Managed by senior management, not the PM.

In construction it is common to set aside 10–15 % of the price. Other industries resist it — the customer may read a visible reserve as a sign of poor planning.

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.9 FMEA as a risk tool
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis is often the first step of a reliability study: review as many components, assemblies, and subsystems as possible to identify failure modes (what can fail and how), their causes, and their effects (the consequences). It is a structured, bottom-up way to surface technical risks before they reach the customer — and it feeds the same probability–impact thinking used above (in FMEA terms, a risk priority number combining severity, occurrence, and detection).

title: 7  Risk Management
text:
7.10 Key Takeaways

A risk is identifiable and can be acted on preemptively; an uncertainty cannot. Risk = Probability × Impact. Opportunities are the positive mirror.
Four stages: identify → analyze → mitigate → control & document (build the knowledge base).
Qualitative: plot risks on a probability–impact matrix; red-zone risks get a written plan before the event.
Quantitative: EMV = probability × impact; decision trees compare choices with chance events; Monte Carlo for whole-network risk.
Responses: accept, minimize, share, transfer, reserve. Pick per risk; ring-fence reserve against the biggest ones.
Task contingency is the PM’s; managerial contingency is management’s, for the truly unforeseeable.
FMEA systematically surfaces technical failure modes, causes, and effects.

Six friends borrow an older car and drive to an unfamiliar beach. The weather forecast is mixed with a chance of rain and high winds; one friend is a very picky eater; the owner plans to replace the car soon due to problems; there is a fireworks show and all-day music at a crowded venue. Problem 2: EMV of competing suppliers

Supplier X: $140 000, 15 % chance of a 3-week slip costing $45 000. Supplier Y: $128 000, 35 % chance of a 3-week slip costing $45 000. On expected cost alone, which is cheaper?
Solution.

X <- 140000 + 0.15 * 45000
Y <- 128000 + 0.35 * 45000
cat(sprintf("Supplier X expected cost: $%s\n", format(X, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("Supplier Y expected cost: $%s\n", format(Y, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("Cheaper on EMV: Supplier %s\n", ifelse(X < Y, "X", "Y")))

Supplier Y expected cost: $143 750
Cheaper on EMV: Supplier Y


X: $146 750. Y: $143 750. Y is cheaper on expected cost — but note X’s risk is less likely, which may matter more than the $3 000 if a slip would blow the holiday launch window. EMV informs the decision; it does not make it.



Problem 3 (discussion): red-zone risk with no cheap mitigation

The “carbon-fibre plant disruption” risk sits in the red zone, but the supplier is the only qualified source and re-qualifying another would take four months you do not have. What are your options?
Discussion points. You cannot minimize the probability much, so work the impact: build a larger contingency reserve (time and money) against it; transfer part of it via contract terms (penalty clauses, guaranteed allocation); share it by co-investing in the supplier’s modernization for priority supply; carry safety stock of the critical carbon-fibre parts; and design a fallback (an aluminium body variant) that could be substituted if the supply fails, accepting a heavier product rather than a missed launch.

8.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
Read and build a Gantt chart and explain what it adds over a network diagram.
Distinguish the four precedence relationships (FS, FF, SS, SF) and use leads and lags.
Combine PERT activity estimates into a project mean and standard deviation.
Calculate the probability of finishing by a target date.
Compute an activity’s crash cost slope and build a least-cost crashing sequence.
Compare crashing and fast-tracking, and state the risks of each.



Before we begin: a schedule is a promise — how confident are you in it?

“The project finishes in 83 days” sounds precise. Is that a date you would bet your bonus on, or a coin flip? This chapter turns a single-number schedule into a probability you can actually stand behind.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
section: 8.2 Introduction: from a network to a calendar
text:
8.2 Introduction: from a network to a calendar
The AON network from Chapter 6 tells you the project takes N days. The schedule puts those days on a calendar, assigns resources, and gives you something to track progress against. The classic tool is the Gantt chart, developed by Henry Gantt between 1910 and 1915 and used at scale for the first time on the Hoover Dam (1931–1936).






Note



Industry snapshot. An automotive program’s master schedule is a Gantt with thousands of rows rolled up to a one-page milestone view for the steering committee. A food-plant install schedule shows the trades stacked so the project manager can see where two crews need the same space on the same day. A defense schedule is baselined and every slip against it is reported.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.3 Gantt charts
A Gantt chart is a time-phased network: it links each activity to a calendar. Linked to a schedule, it also tracks progress against the plan. Benefits: easy to read; shows the network and the schedule together; supports updating and control; useful for assigning resources; and easy to create.

g <- data.frame(
  task = c("A Design outer body", "B Design inner frame", "C Material selection",
           "D Procure motor/controller", "E Wiring harness",
           "F Prototype assembly", "G Drop & EMC test", "H Packaging & approvals"),
  start = c(0, 5, 5, 8, 15, 20, 30, 30),
  dur   = c(5, 8, 3, 12, 5, 10, 8, 12),
  crit  = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
g$end <- g$start + g$dur
g$task <- factor(g$task, levels = rev(g$task))

ggplot(g) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, y = task, yend = task, color = crit),
               linewidth = 8, lineend = "butt") +
  geom_text(aes(x = start + dur / 2, y = task, label = paste0(dur, "d")),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.1 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#C0392B", "FALSE" = "#5DADE2"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "Critical path", "FALSE" = "Has float"),
                     name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "RC-vehicle sub-project schedule", x = "Project day", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 8.1: A Gantt chart for the RC-vehicle sub-project. Bars are activities; the dark segments show the critical path. Arrows (implied by stacking) show that assembly cannot start until design finishes.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.4 Precedence relationships
Most dependencies are finish-to-start, but there are four:








Relationship
Meaning
Example




Finish-to-Start (FS)
B can’t start until A finishes
Build the wall before you paint it


Finish-to-Finish (FF)
B can’t finish until A finishes
Can’t finish editing until writing is finished


Start-to-Start (SS)
B can’t start until A starts (often simultaneous)
Start trimming edges when you start mowing


Start-to-Finish (SF)
A starting triggers B finishing (rare)
The new shift starting ends the old shift



A lead lets a successor start early (overlap); a lag forces a wait (e.g. “wait 2 days for the paint to cure” is FS + 2-day lag).

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.5 Probabilistic scheduling with PERT
A single duration hides uncertainty. Using three-point estimates (Chapter 6), for each activity:
\[t_e = \frac{o + 4m + p}{6}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{p - o}{6}, \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{p - o}{6}\right)^2\]
For the project, sum along the critical path:
\[\mu_{\text{project}} = \sum t_e, \qquad \sigma^2_{\text{project}} = \sum \sigma^2, \qquad \sigma_{\text{project}} = \sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{project}}}\]

8.5.1 Worked Example 1: project duration and its spread
The critical path is A–B–C–D–E with these three-point estimates:

cp <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  o  = c(12, 7, 15, 9, 24),
  m  = c(15, 10, 19, 13, 26),
  p  = c(17, 13, 23, 16, 30)
)
cp$te  <- (cp$o + 4 * cp$m + cp$p) / 6
cp$var <- ((cp$p - cp$o) / 6)^2

mu    <- sum(cp$te)
sigma <- sqrt(sum(cp$var))

cp_show <- cp
cp_show[c("te", "var")] <- lapply(cp_show[c("te", "var")], round, 2)
print(cp_show, row.names = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("\nProject mean duration : %.1f days\n", mu))
cat(sprintf("Project variance      : %.2f\n", sum(cp$var)))
cat(sprintf("Project std deviation : %.2f days\n", sigma))
cat(sprintf("Rough 95%% range        : %.0f to %.0f days\n", mu - 2 * sigma, mu + 2 * sigma))

  A 12 15 17 14.83 0.69
  B  7 10 13 10.00 1.00
  C 15 19 23 19.00 1.78
  D  9 13 16 12.83 1.36
  E 24 26 30 26.33 1.00

Project mean duration : 83.0 days
Project variance      : 5.83
Project std deviation : 2.42 days

8.5.2 Try it yourself: probability of hitting a target date
Standardize the target: \(z = \dfrac{\text{target} - \mu}{\sigma}\), then read the normal cumulative probability.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Why quote “day 86 at 90 % confidence” instead of “day 83”?

Day 83 is the mean — by definition you have only about a 50 % chance of meeting it. Committing to the mean is committing to a coin flip. Adding a buffer to reach 85–90 % confidence is how you turn a schedule into a promise you can keep, and it is the honest version of the “padding” problem from Chapter 9 — one visible buffer at the project level, not hidden padding in every task.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.6 Crashing the schedule
When you crash: the initial schedule was too optimistic; the market wants the product sooner; the project has slipped badly; or the contract rewards finishing early / punishes finishing late.
How you accelerate an activity: improve the productivity of existing resources (focus the team, review best practice); change the working method (swap drawing review for CAD model review); or add resources (overtime, extra shifts, expedited freight).






Warning



Caution on overtime. Research on engineering work found optimal marginal output at about 4 hours of overtime per week; by 10 hours of overtime the marginal extra output had fallen to zero. More hours is not more work.


Every activity has a crash cost slope — the cost to buy back one time unit:
\[\text{slope} = \frac{\text{crash cost} - \text{normal cost}}{\text{normal time} - \text{crash time}}\]

normal_t <- 8; normal_c <- 14000
crash_t  <- 5; crash_c  <- 23000
line <- data.frame(
  t = c(crash_t, normal_t),
  c = c(crash_c, normal_c)
)
ggplot(line, aes(t, c)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E86C1", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#1B4F72") +
  annotate("text", x = normal_t, y = normal_c, label = "Normal point\n(8 wk, $14 000)",
           hjust = 1.1, size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = crash_t, y = crash_c, label = "Crash point\n(5 wk, $23 000)",
           hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = 15500,
           label = "slope = $9 000 / 3 wk\n= $3 000 per week",
           size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "italic", lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(big.mark = " ")) +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = 5:8) +
  labs(title = "Time-cost trade-off for crashing",
       x = "Activity duration (weeks) - shorter to the right",
       y = "Activity cost") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 8.2: Time-cost trade-off for one activity. Between the normal and crash points, buying time gets steadily more expensive per day; past the crash point you cannot buy any more.






8.6.1 Try it yourself: least-cost crashing
To shorten the project, crash critical-path activities in cheapest-slope- first order, one time unit at a time, until you hit the target or run out of crashable critical tasks.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.7 Fast-tracking versus crashing









Crashing
Fast-tracking




Method
Add resources (overtime, staff, expediting)
Overlap tasks that were sequential


Cost
Always adds cost
Little or no added cost


Risk
Diminishing returns; overtime burnout
Rework if the predecessor changes after the successor started



Both only help on the critical path, and after either one you must re-check the network — the critical path can move.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.8 Key Takeaways

A Gantt chart puts the network on a calendar and lets you track progress; it shows activities, dependencies, and resources at once.
Four precedence types: FS (default), FF, SS, SF — with leads (overlap) and lags (forced wait).
PERT project: \(\mu = \sum t_e\) and \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sum \sigma^2}\) along the critical path. The mean is a ~50 % date.
Probability of on-time: \(z = (\text{target} - \mu)/\sigma\), then the normal CDF. Commit to an ~85–90 % date, not the mean.
Crash cost slope \(=\) (crash cost − normal cost) / (normal time − crash time). Crash critical tasks, cheapest slope first.
Crashing buys time with money; fast-tracking buys it with rework risk. Re-check the critical path after either.

title: 8  Project Scheduling
text:
8.9 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Least-cost crash to a deadline

Project critical path A–F–H, currently 23 weeks; the contract needs 20. Crash data: A $513/wk (max 4 wk), F $1 500/wk (max 1 wk), H $950/wk (max 2 wk). Find the least-cost way to remove 3 weeks.
Solution.

crash <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "F", "H"),
  slope = c(513, 1500, 950),
  max = c(4, 1, 2)
)
need <- 3
crash <- crash[order(crash$slope), ]
left <- need; cost <- 0
for (i in seq_len(nrow(crash))) {
  take <- min(left, crash$max[i]); if (take <= 0) break
  cost <- cost + take * crash$slope[i]; left <- left - take
  cat(sprintf("Crash %s by %d wk @ $%d = $%s\n", crash$id[i], take, crash$slope[i],
              format(take * crash$slope[i], big.mark = " ")))
}
cat(sprintf("Total: $%s for %d weeks\n", format(cost, big.mark = " "), need - left))

Crash A by 3 wk @ $513 = $1 539
Total: $1 539 for 3 weeks


Crash A by 3 weeks for $1 539 — far cheaper than touching F or H.



Problem 2: Confidence in a date

A project’s critical path has \(\mu = 60\) days and \(\sigma = 4\) days. The customer wants delivery in 64 days.

What is the probability of meeting day 64? (b) What date should you commit to for 95 % confidence?

Solution.

mu <- 60; sigma <- 4
cat(sprintf("P(finish by day 64) = %.1f%%\n", 100 * pnorm((64 - mu) / sigma)))
cat(sprintf("95%% confident date  = day %.1f\n", mu + qnorm(0.95) * sigma))

P(finish by day 64) = 84.1%
95% confident date  = day 66.6



~84 %. (b) Day 66.6 — commit to day 67.




Problem 3 (discussion): crash or fast-track the RC-vehicle launch?

The retailer moves the launch three weeks earlier. Design is on the critical path and is followed by prototype assembly (also critical). You could add a second designer and pay overtime (crash), or start building the frame jig from the released frame drawings while the body design is still being finalized (fast-track). Which, and why?
Discussion points. Fast-tracking the jig against the frame drawings is low-cost and reasonably safe if the frame design is stable — but if the body design forces a late frame change, the jig is rework. Crashing design with a second modeller adds cost and has coordination overhead (two people on one model), but no rework risk. A common answer: fast-track the clearly stable parts, crash the rest, and hold a contingency for the rework risk you accepted.

9.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
List the common sources of project cost and classify any cost against the four cost dichotomies (direct/indirect, fixed/variable, normal/expedited, recurring/non-recurring).
Calculate direct labour cost from a rate and hours, and apply an indirect-cost percentage.
Select an estimating method (ballpark, parametric, feasibility, definitive) appropriate to the project stage, and state its expected accuracy.
Explain how planning horizon, duration, people, structure, padding, and organizational culture affect estimate quality.
Compare top-down and bottom-up budgeting and build a bottom-up budget from a work breakdown structure using activity-based costing.
Construct a time-phased budget and plot the cumulative cost baseline (the S-curve).
Size a contingency reserve and distinguish it from a management reserve.



Before we begin: you have been asked for “a number” before you have any details

A stakeholder corners you: “Ballpark it — what will this project cost?” You have a one-page concept and nothing else. What do you say, and how do you say it so the number does not follow you around for the next six months as a commitment? Hold that thought.

Back to the running project. Your company must present a budget to Senior Management before the Scope and Charter are approved. The project brief hands you rough ranges to work from:

Cost estimation is the first step in building a budget, and the budget determines whether the project is feasible at all. Two principles run through everything below:

The more clearly you define each cost element up front, the fewer budgeting errors you make.
The more accurate your initial estimate, the more your budget reflects reality — and the less likely a painful overrun later.







Note



Industry snapshot. A defense contractor bidding a firm-fixed-price contract must submit a definitive estimate (±5 %): if the real cost comes in higher, the contractor eats the difference. A food company scoping a new retort line at the concept stage lives with a ballpark (±30 %) and revises as quotes arrive. Same tools, very different tolerance for error — driven by where in the project you are standing.

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
9.3 Where project cost comes from
Cost management starts in the planning phase, when you identify the project’s human and material resources and lay out a time-phased budget that reflects when each will be used. The common sources of cost:

Labour — the project team and anyone charging time to the project.
Materials — everything consumed to build the deliverable.
Subcontractors — external vendors, and internal support departments (test lab, drafting) that cross-charge.
Equipment and facilities — purchased, leased, or allocated.
Travel.
Shipping — inbound and outbound, normal and expedited.

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
9.4 The eight cost types
Every cost gets sorted into one or more of eight categories, arranged as four either/or pairs. A single cost usually carries two or three labels at once.

cost_types <- data.frame(
  Dichotomy = c("Direct vs. Indirect", "", "Fixed vs. Variable", "",
                "Normal vs. Expedited", "", "Recurring vs. Non-recurring", ""),
  Type = c("Direct", "Indirect", "Fixed", "Variable",
           "Normal", "Expedited", "Recurring", "Non-recurring"),
  Meaning = c(
    "Clearly generated by the project (project labour, project materials, POs).",
    "Overhead: rent, property tax, benefits, utilities, depreciation, admin. Often applied as 20--50 % of direct cost.",
    "Does not change with usage (a 6-month equipment lease at a flat fee).",
    "Proportional to usage (machine-hour charges, fuel, mileage).",
    "Incurred during normal operation and working hours; includes overtime that was already scheduled.",
    "Unplanned cost to go faster: rush freight, extra hires, premium to a supplier for priority.",
    "Happens again through the project life: utilities, logistics, ongoing labour, monthly maintenance.",
    "One-time, usually at the start or end: training, prototype tooling, initial market analysis."
  )
)

             caption = "The four cost dichotomies (eight types).") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                            full_width = FALSE) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, bold = TRUE)



Table 9.1: The four cost dichotomies (eight types).






Dichotomy
Type
Meaning




Direct vs. Indirect
Direct
Clearly generated by the project (project labour, project materials, POs).



Indirect
Overhead: rent, property tax, benefits, utilities, depreciation, admin. Often applied as 20--50 % of direct cost.


Fixed vs. Variable
Fixed
Does not change with usage (a 6-month equipment lease at a flat fee).



Variable
Proportional to usage (machine-hour charges, fuel, mileage).


Normal vs. Expedited
Normal
Incurred during normal operation and working hours; includes overtime that was already scheduled.



Expedited

Recurring

9.4.1 Direct labour cost
The core calculation is simple:
\[\text{Total Direct Labour Cost} = \text{Direct Labour Rate} \times \text{Hours Spent}\]
Indirect cost is harder to pin to a task, so many organizations apply it as a percentage of direct cost:
\[\text{Indirect Cost} = \text{Indirect Rate} \times \text{Direct Cost}, \qquad \text{Indirect Rate} \approx 20\%\text{--}50\%\]


9.4.2 Worked Example 1: fully-burdened cost of a work package
The “Design body & frame” work package needs 1 mechanical designer for 220 h at $46/h and 1 junior engineer for 120 h at $32/h. Direct materials for prototypes are $4 500. The company applies indirect cost at 35 % of direct cost.

designer_hours <- 220; designer_rate <- 46
junior_hours   <- 120; junior_rate   <- 32
direct_materials <- 4500
indirect_rate <- 0.35

direct_labour <- designer_hours * designer_rate + junior_hours * junior_rate
direct_cost   <- direct_labour + direct_materials
indirect_cost <- indirect_rate * direct_cost
total_cost    <- direct_cost + indirect_cost

cat("Direct labour  :", sprintf("$%s", format(direct_labour, big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("Direct materials:", sprintf("$%s", format(direct_materials, big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("Direct cost    :", sprintf("$%s", format(direct_cost, big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("Indirect (35%) :", sprintf("$%s", format(indirect_cost, big.mark = " ")), "\n")
cat("-----\n")
cat("Fully-burdened work-package cost:",
    sprintf("$%s", format(round(total_cost), big.mark = " ")), "\n")

Direct labour  : $13 960 
Direct materials: $4 500 
Direct cost    : $18 460 
Indirect (35%) : $6 461 
-----
Fully-burdened work-package cost: $24 921

The pattern: anything charged straight to the project is Direct; overhead is Indirect; anything you pay to go faster is Expedited; anything paid once is Non-recurring. Most items are genuinely two or three of these at once.



9.4.3 The dichotomies on the running project

Fixed vs. variable. The 6-month lease on the CMM is fixed — the fee is the same whether you measure 50 parts or 5 000. The machine-hour charge on the rented moulding press is variable. Leasing an expensive machine is a real PM judgement call: will the usage justify the flat fee?
Normal vs. expedited. Air-freighting circuit boards from the supplier to recover a slipped date is expedited and direct. The overtime you planned into the schedule from day one is still normal.
Recurring vs. non-recurring. Prototype tooling and the initial market analysis are non-recurring. Utilities, logistics, and the team’s salaries are recurring — and it matters which is which the moment you build a time-phased budget.

9.5 Estimating methods and their accuracy
The method you can use depends on how much you know, which depends on how far into the project you are.

  `When` = c(

    "A genuinely similar past project exists, with reliable archived actuals.",
    "Scope is clear and first supplier quotes are back (common in construction).",
    "Most design is complete; major POs can be written; detail is known."
  ),
  Accuracy = c("+/- 30 %", "+/- 15 %", "+/- 10 %", "+/- 5 %"),
  check.names = FALSE

This is the cone of uncertainty: the possible range around an estimate is widest at the concept stage and narrows as the project is defined.

cone <- data.frame(
  stage = factor(c("Ballpark", "Parametric", "Feasibility", "Definitive"),
                 levels = c("Ballpark", "Parametric", "Feasibility", "Definitive")),
  x = 1:4,

point_estimate <- 1.0  # $M

ggplot(cone, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = point_estimate * (1 - err),
                  ymax = point_estimate * (1 + err)),
              fill = "#5DADE2", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 + err)), linewidth = 1, color = "#2E86C1") +
  geom_line(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 - err)), linewidth = 1, color = "#2E86C1") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.7, xend = 4.3, y = point_estimate, yend = point_estimate,
           linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.3, y = point_estimate, label = "point estimate  $1.0M",
           hjust = 1, vjust = -0.7, size = 3.3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  geom_point(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 + err)), size = 2.5, color = "#1B4F72") +
  geom_point(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 - err)), size = 2.5, color = "#1B4F72") +
  geom_text(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 + err),
                label = paste0("+", scales::percent(err, accuracy = 1))),
            vjust = -0.8, size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale) +
  geom_text(aes(y = point_estimate * (1 - err),
                label = paste0("-", scales::percent(err, accuracy = 1))),
            vjust = 1.6, size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = levels(cone$stage)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "M", big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(title = "The cone of uncertainty", x = NULL, y = "Estimated project cost") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 9.1: The cone of uncertainty. Early estimates can be off by +/- 30 %; the range narrows to +/- 5 % only once most design decisions are locked. The same $1.0M point estimate means very different things at each stage.






9.5.1 Try it yourself: parametric estimate and the accuracy band
A parametric estimate uses a cost-estimating relationship (CER) from history — for example, “past RC-vehicle projects cost about $14.50 per assembled part plus $85 000 of fixed project cost.” The live cell builds the estimate and shows the band each method would put around it.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Why quote a range at all — why not just give “the number”?

Because a single number reads as a commitment. If you say “$1.8M” at the concept stage and the definitive estimate later lands at $2.0M, you have “overrun by $200k” — even though $2.0M was always inside the ±30 % ballpark band. Quoting “$1.3M–$2.3M, ballpark” sets the expectation honestly and buys you room to refine. A clear distinction between an estimate and a commitment is one of the most important things a PM can establish early.

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
section: 9.6 What makes estimates good or bad
text:
9.6 What makes estimates good or bad







Factor
Effect on estimate quality




Planning horizon
Estimates of near-term work are close to 100 % accurate; accuracy falls the further out the task sits.


Project duration
Long projects and new technology add uncertainty, especially if the scope statement is weak.


People
The closer the estimator’s experience matches the work, the better. Teams that have worked together before form faster. Staff turnover hurts.


Structure
Dedicated teams deliver faster but tie up people full-time. Matrix organizations are more cost-efficient but slower.


Padding
Estimators add a safety margin. If everyone pads a little, the project total is badly overstated and stops reflecting reality.


Organizational culture
Some cultures reward padding; others prize accuracy. The consequences an estimator faces for a miss shape the number they give.


Other
Equipment downtime, sickness, vacation, holidays, legal limits, and project priority all leak into the estimate.




9.6.1 The cost of padding
Padding feels prudent per task. Watch what it does across a whole project.

set.seed(2025)
n_tasks <- 40
true_mean <- 40           # hours, honest most-likely per task
# Honest estimates vary around the truth; padded estimates add 15% on top.
honest  <- rnorm(n_tasks, true_mean, 6)
padded  <- honest * 1.15

df <- data.frame(
  task = 1:n_tasks,
  honest_cum = cumsum(honest),
  padded_cum = cumsum(padded)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = task)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = honest_cum, color = "Honest estimate"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = padded_cum, color = "Every task padded 15%"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = n_tasks, y = df$padded_cum[n_tasks],
           label = paste0("+", round(100 * (df$padded_cum[n_tasks] /
                          df$honest_cum[n_tasks] - 1)), "% on the total"),
           hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, size = 3.4 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Honest estimate" = "#27AE60",
                                "Every task padded 15%" = "#C0392B")) +
  labs(title = "Per-task padding compounds into a meaningless total",
       x = "Cumulative task count", y = "Cumulative estimated hours",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 9.2: A 15 % ‘just to be safe’ pad added to every one of 40 tasks does not add 15 % to the project — it adds 15 % to the mean, but the padded total sits far above any realistic outcome because the pads do not all get used.





The fix is not “ban all safety margin” — it is to remove padding from the work packages and hold a single, visible contingency reserve at the project level (covered below).


9.6.2 Guidelines for estimating (cost and time)

Responsibility: the person who will do the task makes the estimate (except for highly specialised work). It uses their experience and builds their buy-in.
Use several estimators: independent estimates from knowledgeable people, reconciled, remove the extremes.
Assume normal conditions: normal hours, normal resource levels — and write the assumptions down.
Define the time units and the estimating base.
Estimate each task independently; be careful with chains of dependent tasks, and keep one estimator per task.
Keep contingencies out of the work packages. Contingency is a separate, managed fund.

text:
9.7 Budgeting: top-down and bottom-up
The budget and the schedule are built in tandem — the budget decides whether the schedule’s milestones are reachable.

  Aspect = c("How it starts", "Advantages", "Disadvantages"),
  `Top-down` = c(

  ),

    "Forces detailed planning; improves PM--functional-manager communication; gives management a clear basis for prioritizing scarce resources.",
    "Reduces management's control to oversight rather than initiation; can misalign project goals with company goals; fine-tuning is time-consuming."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE

text:
9.8 Activity-based costing (ABC)
ABC treats a project as a series of activities, each of which consumes resources. Cost the activities and you have costed the project. Four steps:

Identify the activities that consume resources and assign costs to them.
Identify the cost drivers for each activity (personnel, materials, machine time…).
Compute a cost rate per driver unit (e.g. labour $/hour).
Assign cost = rate × units the project uses. (Example: an engineer at $60/h working 80 h = $4 800.)


9.8.1 A preliminary ABC budget
Splitting each activity into its direct and overhead components:

  Overhead   = c(500, 1000, 500, 750, 2000, 1250)

abc$Total <- abc$Direct + abc$Overhead
abc <- rbind(abc, data.frame(Activity = "TOTAL",

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
section: 9.9 The time-phased budget and the S-curve
text:
9.9 The time-phased budget and the S-curve
A time-phased budget spreads each activity’s cost across the calendar periods when it will actually be spent. Summing down the columns gives monthly planned spend; the running total is the cumulative cost baseline — the S-curve you will track the project against in Chapter 12.

phased <- data.frame(
  month = factor(c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May"),
                 levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May")),
  Survey       = c(4000, 3000,     0,     0,    0),
  Design       = c(   0, 5000,  8000,     0,    0),
  ClearSite    = c(   0, 1000,  4000,  2000,    0),
  Foundation   = c(   0,    0,  3000,  4000,    0),
  Framing      = c(   0,    0,     0,  3000, 4000),
  PlumbWire    = c(   0,    0,     0,     0, 2000)
)
phased$monthly <- rowSums(phased[, -1])
phased$cumulative <- cumsum(phased$monthly)

scale_factor <- max(phased$cumulative) / max(phased$monthly)

ggplot(phased, aes(x = month)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = monthly), fill = "#5DADE2", width = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cumulative / scale_factor, group = 1),
            color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cumulative / scale_factor), color = "#C0392B", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(y = cumulative / scale_factor,
                label = scales::dollar(cumulative, big.mark = " ")),
            vjust = -1, size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, color = "#C0392B") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Planned spend this month",
    labels = scales::dollar_format(big.mark = " "),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * scale_factor, name = "Cumulative baseline (S-curve)",
                        labels = scales::dollar_format(big.mark = " "))
  ) +
  labs(title = "Time-phased budget and cumulative cost baseline", x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 9.3: Time-phased budget for a six-activity project. Bars are planned spend per month; the line is the cumulative baseline (the S-curve). Spend is slow at first, steepest mid-project, and tapers at the end.





Matching the cost baseline to the schedule baseline is what lets you set milestones for both schedule and budget and later tell whether a project that has spent 60 % of its money is 60 %, 40 %, or 80 % done.

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
9.10 Contingency reserves
A budget contingency is extra money set aside to cover the uncertainty that every estimate carries — because even the best budget is only an estimate and something unforeseen always happens. Key points:

Added after all costs are identified, as a cushion on top of the calculated total (commonly 10–15 %; the MGMT-3105 Costs Chart uses 15 %).
Not included in an ABC budget — it sits on top.
The PM controls a project contingency fund; separately, top management holds a management reserve for genuinely unknown-unknown events.

Why stakeholders push back: the percentage can look arbitrary, or feel like being asked to pay for the vendor’s poor cost control. Decide early — and write into the scope statement — whether contingency applies across all tasks or is held for the tasks critical to project success.

reserves <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("Covers", "Owned by", "Part of the cost baseline?", "Typical size"),
  `Contingency reserve` = c(
    "Identified risks / \"known-unknowns\" (small scope adjustments, iteration, Murphy's Law).",
    "Project manager.",
    "Yes --- inside the baseline.",
    "10--15 % of estimated cost (project-dependent)."
  ),
  `Management reserve` = c(
    "Unidentified risks / \"unknown-unknowns.\"",
    "Senior management / sponsor.",
    "No --- outside the baseline; released by management.",
    "Set by organizational policy."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(reserves, align = c("l", "l", "l"),
             caption = "Contingency reserve vs. management reserve.") |>

How would top-down vs. bottom-up change this number?

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
9.11 Key Takeaways

Cost management starts in planning. Sources: labour, materials, subcontractors, equipment/facilities, travel, shipping.
Every cost carries two or three of the eight labels: direct/indirect, fixed/variable, normal/expedited, recurring/non-recurring. Direct labour cost = rate × hours; indirect is often 20–50 % of direct.
Estimating method follows project stage: ballpark ±30 %, parametric ±15 %, feasibility ±10 %, definitive ±5 % — the cone of uncertainty. Always quote a range, and keep “estimate” separate from “commitment.”
Estimate quality is driven by planning horizon, duration, people, structure, culture, and padding — which compounds into a meaningless total. Remove pads from work packages; hold one visible contingency.
Top-down imposes discipline but breeds friction; bottom-up (via activity-based costing on the WBS) forces real planning. ABC = identify activities → cost drivers → rate per unit → rate × units.
A time-phased budget produces the cumulative cost baseline (S-curve) you track against later.
Contingency reserve (10–15 %, PM-owned, inside the baseline, covers known-unknowns) is distinct from the management reserve (sponsor-owned, outside the baseline, covers unknown-unknowns). Contingency is added after ABC, never inside it.

title: 9  Cost Estimation and Budgeting
text:
9.12 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Fully-burdened labour and an indirect-rate swing

A test campaign needs 2 technicians for 3 weeks (37.5 h/week each) at $34/h, plus $6 200 of consumables. Compute the fully-burdened cost at an indirect rate of 25 %, and again at 45 %. How much does the indirect-rate assumption alone move the number?
Solution.

techs <- 2; weeks <- 3; hrs_week <- 37.5; rate <- 34
consumables <- 6200

direct_labour <- techs * weeks * hrs_week * rate
direct_cost   <- direct_labour + consumables

for (ir in c(0.25, 0.45)) {
  total <- direct_cost * (1 + ir)
  cat(sprintf("Indirect %2.0f%%:  direct $%s  +  indirect $%s  =  $%s\n",
              ir * 100,
              format(direct_cost, big.mark = " "),
              format(round(direct_cost * ir), big.mark = " "),
              format(round(total), big.mark = " ")))
}
cat(sprintf("\nSwing from the indirect-rate assumption alone: $%s\n",
            format(round(direct_cost * (0.45 - 0.25)), big.mark = " ")))

Indirect 25%:  direct $13 850  +  indirect $3 462  =  $17 312
Indirect 45%:  direct $13 850  +  indirect $6 232  =  $20 082

Swing from the indirect-rate assumption alone: $2 770


The direct cost is fixed at $21 500, but the burdened total moves by $4 300 — 20 % of direct — purely on the overhead assumption. Always state the indirect rate you used.



Problem 2: Which estimating method, and what range?

For each situation, name the method and give the ± band around a $500 000 point estimate.

A retailer asks, in a hallway, roughly what a new product line will cost. You have a concept sketch.
You have run three near-identical RC-vehicle launches in the last four years with clean cost records.
All major POs are drafted and 90 % of the design is released for a firm-fixed-price defense bid.

Solution.


Ballpark, ±30 % → $350 000 – $650 000.


Comparative/parametric, ±15 % → $425 000 – $575 000.


Definitive, ±5 % → $475 000 – $525 000. (Anything looser is a bad idea on a fixed-price bid.)





Problem 3: Variance analysis on the ABC budget

Using the preliminary ABC budget above (total planned $63 250), the project finishes with these actuals: Survey $4 250, Design $8 000, Clear site $3 500, Foundation $8 500, Framing $11 250, Plumb & wire $5 150. Find the variance per activity and overall, and flag the activities that need a post-mortem.
Solution.

planned <- c(Survey = 4000, Design = 8000, `Clear site` = 4000,
             Foundation = 7500, Framing = 10000, `Plumb & wire` = 5000)
actual  <- c(4250, 8000, 3500, 8500, 11250, 5150)

variance <- planned - actual            # + = under budget
tab <- data.frame(Activity = names(planned),
                  Planned = as.integer(planned),
                  Actual = as.integer(actual),
                  Variance = as.integer(variance),
                  Pct = round(100 * variance / planned, 1))
print(tab, row.names = FALSE)

cat(sprintf("\nTOTAL planned $%s  actual $%s  variance $%s (%.1f%%)\n",
            format(sum(planned), big.mark = " "),
            format(sum(actual),  big.mark = " "),
            format(sum(variance), big.mark = " "),
            100 * sum(variance) / sum(planned)))

     Activity Planned Actual Variance   Pct
       Survey    4000   4250     -250  -6.2
       Design    8000   8000        0   0.0
   Clear site    4000   3500      500  12.5
   Foundation    7500   8500    -1000 -13.3
      Framing   10000  11250    -1250 -12.5
 Plumb & wire    5000   5150     -150  -3.0

TOTAL planned $38 500  actual $40 650  variance $-2 150 (-5.6%)


Design and (roughly) Survey held. Foundation (-13 %) and Framing (-13 %) blew through and drove the whole project $2 150 (3.4 %) over — those two get the post-mortem.



Problem 4 (discussion): sizing contingency for the RC-vehicle project

The project brief flags several live risks: one candidate motor supplier is unproven, that supplier’s staff are negotiating a first labour contract, the carbon-fibre supplier is mid-restructuring after an acquisition, and a new assembly line would carry a learning curve. The subtotal budget is $620 000.
Would you size the contingency at 10 %, 15 %, or 20 %? Would you spread it across all tasks or ring-fence it for specific ones? Defend your answer.
Discussion points. With that many concentrated, plausible risks, 10 % is light; 15 % is defensible and matches the course’s Costs Chart; 20 % is arguable if the unproven-supplier and new-line risks are both realised. A strong answer ring-fences most of the reserve against the supplier and assembly-line line items (the tasks critical to success) rather than smearing it evenly, and states that split in the scope statement so stakeholders are not surprised when it is drawn down.

text:

Before we begin: recall a negotiation you “won” but regretted

Did you win the point and lose the relationship? Most project negotiations are with people you will work with again next week. That constraint changes everything.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
section: 10.2 Introduction: the project manager negotiates every day
text:
10.2 Introduction: the project manager negotiates every day
As a project manager your day is full of negotiation, inside and outside the organization. You negotiate for or with:

Resources — material, time, equipment, money
Contractors — costs, delivery schedules, quality of material, hours of work
Department managers — manpower, schedules

On the RC-vehicle project the sharp negotiations are obvious: the motor and control-system supply contract (trusted MCS, now moving production to Mexico, vs. unproven Paragon four hours away with staff negotiating a first labour contract), and the recurring fight with functional managers over which engineers you get and for how long.






Note



Industry snapshot. An automotive buyer negotiating a multi-year harness contract is really negotiating the whole package — price, tooling ownership, capacity guarantees, engineering support, payment terms. A defense subcontract negotiation is bounded by regulation (allowable cost, audit rights). In a food company, the PM negotiating a sanitation window with operations is negotiating downtime, which is money.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.3 The negotiation mindset

Separate the people from the problem. Everyone has ego, fears, insecurities — do not tap into the other side’s, or you lose control of both sides.
Stick to business. Keep personalities out of it; a charm offensive fools no one.
Put yourself in their shoes. Nobody likes a direct attack; it is counter-productive.
Win-win or no win. Talk money last if possible; a negotiation is about the whole package, not just the number.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.4 Getting ready
There are three stages — before, during, after — and before should be the biggest.
Gather information about the other side: their vital interests, goals, costs, strategies, positions, needs; their product strengths; concession patterns; past negotiating style; their bottom line; corporate deadlines and time constraints; their budget; geographic limits. Also know your own position, the players, and who holds the power — including people behind the scenes.
Develop strategy: aim high (with more than one win-win scenario in mind); be realistic; rank your objectives by priority; know your bottom line; decide whether deadlock or termination are tolerable outcomes; separate the necessary items from the expendable; have a few red herrings ready; plan how to help the other side sell the deal internally; find where your interests and theirs intersect.
Write the plan and an agenda: your interests and theirs; your desired outcomes and your estimate of theirs; your authority limits and theirs; any fact sheet either side needs. The agenda names the meeting’s goal, is published in advance, and lists invitees and location.

10.4.1 The three questions — and who controls the room
Every negotiator should ask: How much power do I have? What time pressure is there? Do I trust the other side?
And: who controls a conversation? Generally the person asking the questions, because they set the direction. Aim to ask most of the questions — politely — and recognise when it is being done to you.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.5 BATNA, reservation point, and ZOPA

BATNA — your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. What you will do if this deal falls through. A strong BATNA is your real source of power.
Reservation point — the worst deal you would still accept (a buyer’s maximum price, a seller’s minimum price), set by your BATNA.
ZOPA — the Zone Of Possible Agreement: the overlap between the two reservation points. If there is no overlap, no deal is possible at those terms.


10.5.1 Worked Example 1: is there a ZOPA?
You are buying the motor/controller package. Your BATNA (Paragon’s quote plus the cost of the risk it carries) puts your reservation price at $168 000 — you would not pay MCS more than that. MCS’s floor, given their costs and other customers, is $150 000.

buyer_reservation  <- 168000   # most you will pay
seller_reservation <- 150000   # least they will accept

if (seller_reservation <= buyer_reservation) {
  zopa_low  <- seller_reservation
  zopa_high <- buyer_reservation
  cat(sprintf("ZOPA exists: $%s to $%s  (width $%s)\n",
              format(zopa_low, big.mark = " "),
              format(zopa_high, big.mark = " "),
              format(zopa_high - zopa_low, big.mark = " ")))
  cat("Any agreed price in that band beats both sides' alternatives.\n")
} else {
  cat("No ZOPA -- the seller's floor is above the buyer's ceiling. Change the package or walk.\n")
}

ZOPA exists: $150 000 to $168 000  (width $18 000)
Any agreed price in that band beats both sides' alternatives.




10.5.2 Try it yourself: reservation points from a BATNA

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Why does improving your BATNA move the whole negotiation?

Your reservation point is set by your BATNA. If you pre-qualify a credible second supplier (a better BATNA), your reservation price drops — you can credibly walk at a lower number — which shifts the ZOPA and the likely settlement in your favour, without saying a word at the table. The best negotiating move often happens before the meeting, in the form of a real alternative.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.6 Language and tells
A few sample moves: “My colleagues and I cannot settle for that” (establish power early); “What are you looking for in these negotiations?” (make them open first); “Do you have the authority to commit to that?” (probe their authority); “Let’s set that aside and come back to it” (avoid a hard no).
And listen past the words. “To be brutally honest…” and “To tell you the truth…” often precede a lie. “Off the record…” — nothing is off the record; the negotiation is always on. Watch congruence: when words and body language disagree, believe the body language.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.7 Conflict management
Conflict “begins when you perceive that someone has frustrated, or is about to frustrate, a major concern of yours.” It is perceptual (it doesn’t matter whether a wrong was actually done, only that it is perceived) and dynamic (the original cause may no longer matter, yet the conflict persists).
Three types on projects:

Goal-oriented — disagreement over end results, scope outcomes, specs, priorities. Fuelled by vague goals that let people fill in their own interpretation (and hidden agendas).
Administrative — who has authority or control over functions, tasks, and decisions. The matrix structure breeds this — everyone has two bosses.
Interpersonal — personality differences: work ethic, behavioural style, ego, personalities that don’t mesh.


10.7.1 Three views of conflict








School
View
Response




Traditional
All conflict is bad
Suppress and eliminate it, fast


Behavioral
Conflict is natural and inevitable
Accept it and manage it well


Interactionist
A controlled amount of conflict is beneficial
Encourage some — it prevents stagnation and drives innovation; too little = inertia, too much = chaos





10.7.2 Sources, ranked by intensity

cs <- data.frame(
  source = c("Schedules", "Project priorities", "Resources", "Technical opinions",
             "Administrative procedures", "Cost", "Personality"),
  intensity = 7:1
)
cs$source <- factor(cs$source, levels = rev(cs$source))
ggplot(cs, aes(intensity, source)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5DADE2", width = 0.68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = intensity), hjust = -0.4, size = 3.6 * diagram_text_scale) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 8), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(title = "What project teams actually fight about",
       x = "Relative intensity (7 = highest)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 10.1: Sources of project conflict ranked by typical intensity (from PMBOK data). Schedules, priorities, and resources dominate; personality is last – it is usually the first thing blamed and rarely the real cause.





Organizational causes: reward systems (functional managers hoard their best people), scarce resources, uncertainty (weak matrix — unclear who is in charge), different mindsets among departments. Interpersonal causes: misconceptions about others’ behaviour, faulty communication (often style, not content), personal grudges.

“It only becomes personal when the root cause of the conflict is not resolved. Personality is very frequently the first diagnosis” — and usually the wrong one.



10.7.3 Conflict-resolution methods (PMBOK)








Method
What it is
Best when




Confronting (problem-solving)
Solve the real, underlying problem
There is time and goodwill; the durable fix


Compromising
Each side gives something; partial satisfaction for both
Positions are far apart and a deadline looms


Withdrawal / avoidance
Retreat or postpone
The issue is trivial, or emotions need to cool


Smoothing
Emphasize agreement, play down differences
Preserving the relationship matters more right now


Forcing
Push one view at the other’s expense
A true emergency, or a matter of safety/ethics

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.8 Key Takeaways

PMs negotiate constantly — for resources, with contractors, with functional managers. Before is the biggest stage; prepare more than you think you need.
Separate people from the problem, focus on interests not positions, aim for win-win or no win, and talk money last.
BATNA sets your reservation point; the overlap of both reservation points is the ZOPA. No ZOPA, no deal — improve your BATNA or change the package.
The person asking the questions usually controls the conversation.
Project conflict is perceptual and dynamic. Types: goal-oriented, administrative, interpersonal. The interactionist view holds that a controlled amount of conflict is healthy.
Teams fight most about schedules, priorities, and resources — personality is last and is usually a misdiagnosis of an unresolved root cause.
Match the resolution method — confronting, compromising, withdrawal, smoothing, forcing — to the situation; confronting is the durable fix.

title: 10  Negotiation and Conflict Management
text:
10.9 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Name the cause of conflict

Which cause does each statement point to?

“I can’t talk to her after what her son said to my son.” → Personal grudge (interpersonal).
“Sales management here are lazy — they always leave by 4:00.” → Different mindsets among departments (organizational).
“She barely looked at my report; she’s already decided to ignore it.” → Misconceptions about others’ behaviour (interpersonal).
“Our computers are slow because their division always gets the best ones.” → Scarce resources (organizational).
“The worse your project does at year-end, the better mine looks.” → Reward systems (organizational).
“Why should I do that for the PM if my functional manager didn’t tell me?” → Uncertainty / two bosses (organizational, matrix).




Problem 2: ZOPA and a walk-away

You will pay at most $95 000 for a tooling package (your BATNA: build it in-house for $98 000). The vendor’s floor is $102 000.

Is there a ZOPA? (b) What are your options?

Solution.

buyer_max  <- 95000
seller_min <- 102000
cat(ifelse(seller_min <= buyer_max, "ZOPA exists", "No ZOPA"), "\n")
cat(sprintf("Gap to close: $%s\n", format(seller_min - buyer_max, big.mark = " ")))

No ZOPA 
Gap to close: $7 000



No — the vendor’s floor is $7 000 above your ceiling. (b) Exercise your BATNA (build in-house at $98 000), expand the package so the vendor’s per-unit economics improve, split tooling ownership, or find a third vendor.




Problem 3 (discussion): the functional manager skips your stand-up

The maintenance supervisor on your project has missed the first two morning meetings. How could this signal each of: reward systems, scarce resources, uncertainty, different mindsets, misconceptions, faulty communication, personal grudge?
Discussion points. Reward systems: their boss doesn’t value project work, so they deprioritize it. Scarce resources: they are triple-booked and the meeting lost. Uncertainty: they are not sure the meeting applies to them. Different mindsets: maintenance culture sees planning meetings as talk, not work. Misconceptions: they think you have already sidelined their input. Faulty communication: the invite never reached them, or the time was ambiguous. Grudge: a past project soured them on you. The point: do not jump to the grudge — confront it by asking, and you will usually find one of the structural causes.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
