Before we begin: your plan assumed the person was free — were they?

Almost every first-draft project schedule is built as if the organization has unlimited trained people standing by. It never does. This chapter is what happens when the plan meets the staffing reality.

title: 11  Resource Management
section: 11.2 Introduction: the optimism of the first schedule
text:
11.2 Introduction: the optimism of the first schedule
The RC-vehicle schedule from Chapter 8 quietly assumed every resource was available exactly when needed. Reality: there is one CMM for validation, the millwrights are shared with production, the design engineers are borrowed from a functional department, and the new assembly line has a learning curve. Building plans under the assumption of unlimited resources inevitably leads to schedule slippage and extra cost as reality overtakes the optimism.
Projects run inside three kinds of constraint — technical, physical, and resource — and this chapter is about the last one: people, materials, space, money, equipment.






Note



Industry snapshot. An automotive company with one set of climate chambers watches validation projects stack up behind that single resource — the classic bottleneck. A food plant schedules every project around the one weekend sanitation window. A defense program’s cleared personnel are a fixed pool, so every new task is a reallocation, not an addition.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.3 Resource loading and the histogram
A resource histogram plots how much of a resource is required over time. Stack each activity’s demand day by day and the over-allocations jump out — provided you remember the chart assumes each person is available 100 % of the time, which is rarely true.

days <- 1:14
before <- c(6,6,6,6,6, 9,9,9,9,10, 8,10,9,7)
after  <- c(6,6,6,6,6, 9,9,9,9,9,  9,9,9,7)
df <- data.frame(
  day = rep(days, 2),
  people = c(before, after),
  state = rep(c("Before leveling", "After leveling"), each = length(days))
)
df$state <- factor(df$state, levels = c("Before leveling", "After leveling"))

ggplot(df, aes(day, people)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = people > 9), width = 0.75) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 9, linetype = "dashed", color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 9.6, label = "limit = 9/day",
           color = "#C0392B", size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#5DADE2", "TRUE" = "#C0392B"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~state, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = days) +
  labs(title = "Leveling removes the over-allocation peak",
       x = "Project day", y = "People required") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9.5 * diagram_text_scale)
  )







Figure 11.1: Resource histogram before and after leveling, against a limit of 9 people/day. Leveling shifts a task with float so the peak on day 12 no longer breaches the limit – without extending the project.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.4 Resource leveling

PMBOK: a technique in which start and finish dates are adjusted based on resource constraints, with the goal of balancing demand for resources against the available supply.

Two objectives: (1) make sure resources are available at the right time, and (2) let each activity run with the smoothest possible transitions across resource-usage levels.
When you must choose which activity to move, work through them in this order:

Activities with the smallest float
Activities with the smallest duration
Activities with the lowest ID (earliest in the WBS)
Activities with the most successors
Activities requiring the most resources


11.4.1 Worked Example 1: which task do you move?
Day 12 needs 10 people against a limit of 9. Four activities are running that day:

running_day12 <- data.frame(
  task = c("D", "E", "H", "J"),
  float = c(12, 0, 0, 5),
  duration = c(6, 6, 7, 3),
  successors = c(1, 2, 1, 0),
  people = c(3, 3, 3, 1)
)
print(running_day12, row.names = FALSE)

# Only tasks with float can move without extending the project.
movable <- running_day12[running_day12$float > 0, ]
# Among movable tasks, prefer smallest float, then smallest duration.
pick <- movable[order(movable$float, movable$duration), ][1, ]
cat(sprintf("\nMovable tasks: %s\n", paste(movable$task, collapse = ", ")))
cat(sprintf("Move first: task %s (float %d, duration %d) -- shift it later within its slack.\n",
            pick$task, pick$float, pick$duration))
cat("E and H are on the critical path (float 0) -- moving them would extend the project.\n")

 task float duration successors people
    D    12        6          1      3
    E     0        6          2      3
    H     0        7          1      3
    J     5        3          0      1

Movable tasks: D, J
Move first: task J (float 5, duration 3) -- shift it later within its slack.
E and H are on the critical path (float 0) -- moving them would extend the project.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.5 Time-constrained vs. resource-constrained

Time-constrained: the end date is fixed; you add or reassign resources to protect it (this is closer to smoothing).
Resource-constrained: the resource limit is fixed; if leveling within float is not enough, the project duration extends (undesirable, but sometimes unavoidable).

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.6 Resource smoothing
Smoothing is done after leveling and never extends the project duration. It uses available float to even out resource usage — filling the valleys from the peaks.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.7 Splitting a task
Splitting means interrupting continuous work on an activity, moving that resource to another activity, then returning. It helps only when there are no large start-up or shutdown costs, and only some tasks can be split at all (you cannot pause a concrete pour).

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.8 The multi-project resource problem
Organizations rarely buy new resources for each project — they share them across projects. The core challenge is interdependency: a resource decision in one project ripples into others. Common problems:

Inefficient use of resources
Resource bottlenecks
Ripple effects
Heightened pressure on people to multitask

Any multi-project scheduling system tries to minimize three things:

Schedule slippage — often carrying real financial penalty clauses per day late.
Resource utilization losses — the unused-capacity gap; the goal is to fill it with other projects’ work.
In-process inventory (WIP) — work waiting on an unavailable resource, stacked behind a bottleneck (e.g. one shared climate chamber).


wk <- 1:14
used <- c(3,4,5,6,6,7,7,6,5,5,4,3,3,2)
cap  <- 8
df <- data.frame(wk, used, unused = cap - used)
df_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(df, c(used, unused), names_to = "kind", values_to = "res")
df_long$kind <- factor(df_long$kind, levels = c("unused", "used"),
                        labels = c("Unused capacity", "Used by this project"))

ggplot(df_long, aes(wk, res, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = cap, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Used by this project" = "#5DADE2",

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.9 Sustainability and resources
Resource management is not only about people-hours. The circular-economy thinking from Chapter 1 applies directly: minimize raw material use, prefer recyclable and local inputs, design the project so equipment and tooling can be reused on the next program, and track material and energy as managed resources with their own KPIs — not just labour and money.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.10 Key Takeaways

Projects run inside technical, physical, and resource constraints; resources are people, materials, space, money, equipment.
A resource histogram exposes over-allocation (against a 100 %-availability assumption).
Leveling shifts tasks within their float to respect a resource limit; move tasks in order of smallest float → smallest duration → lowest ID → most successors → most resources. Critical-path tasks have no float, so moving them extends the project.
Time-constrained protects the date with resources; resource-constrained may extend the date.
Smoothing happens after leveling, uses float, and never extends duration.
Splitting helps only when start-up/shutdown costs are low and the task can be split.
Multi-project sharing creates bottlenecks, ripple effects, and multitasking pressure; minimize slippage, utilization loss, and WIP, and pick a priority rule deliberately.
Multitasking is not free — “40 hours” of nominal capacity is far less once someone carries several projects.

title: 11  Resource Management
text:
11.11 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Level to the limit

Day 10 requires 10 people; the limit is 9. Running that day: task C (float 4, duration 5, 4 people), task D (float 0, duration 6, 3 people), task F (float 0, duration 6, 3 people). Which task moves, and what is the risk if none can?
Solution.

d10 <- data.frame(task = c("C", "D", "F"),
                  float = c(4, 0, 0), dur = c(5, 6, 6), ppl = c(4, 3, 3))
mov <- d10[d10$float > 0, ]
cat("Only task with float:", mov$task, "\n")
cat("Move C into its 4 days of slack -> day-10 demand drops to 6, under the limit.\n")
cat("If C could not move (no split, hard dependency), the project duration extends.\n")

Only task with float: C 
Move C into its 4 days of slack -> day-10 demand drops to 6, under the limit.
If C could not move (no split, hard dependency), the project duration extends.





Problem 2: Does this need leveling or smoothing?

A resource has a 40 h/week limit. Weekly demand over 6 weeks is 55, 20, 48, 15, 50, 22 h. Total 210 h.
Solution.

demand <- c(55, 20, 48, 15, 50, 22); limit <- 40
flat <- sum(demand) / length(demand)
cat(sprintf("Even spread: %.1f h/week vs limit %d\n", flat, limit))
cat(ifelse(flat <= limit,
           "Fits if spread evenly -> smoothing (shift within float) can solve it.\n",
           "Still over even when flat -> leveling (extend) or add resource.\n"))

Even spread: 35.0 h/week vs limit 40
Fits if spread evenly -> smoothing (shift within float) can solve it.


35 h/week average is under the 40 h limit, so smoothing within float can solve it without extending the project.



Problem 3 (discussion): the shared CMM bottleneck

Three projects, including yours, all need the single CMM for final validation in the same two-week window. Using the priority rules, how would you decide the order, and what could reduce the bottleneck?
Discussion points. Apply a rule and be explicit about it: minimum late finish (whichever project has the tightest deadline goes first) is defensible if one launch date is immovable; greatest resource demand surfaces the bottleneck earliest. Reduce it by: staggering the validation tasks into each project’s float, renting a second CMM for the peak, outsourcing some measurement to a metrology lab, or moving non-CMM checks off the critical window so the CMM time is used only for what truly needs it.

12.2 Introduction: from a plan to a control system
You have planned the RC-vehicle project — scope, WBS, schedule, budget. It is now week 8. The sponsor asks the only question that matters at this stage: are we on track, and if not, how far off, and what will it cost to finish?
Answering that needs a control system: a closed loop that measures progress, compares it to the baseline, analyzes the variance, and drives a corrective action — then measures again.

The reference for “compare” is the performance measurement baseline — the approved scope + schedule + cost locked in at the end of planning (Chapter 9’s S-curve is its cost dimension).






Note



Industry snapshot. Earned value management is contractually mandated on large U.S. defense programs (EIA-748). Automotive programs run a lighter version at the milestone level. A food-plant capital project tracks committed vs. spent vs. installed. The math below is the same at every scale.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.3 The three curves
Earned value management tracks three cumulative quantities against time:








Term
Also called
Meaning




PV — Planned Value
BCWS
The budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now


EV — Earned Value
BCWP
The budgeted cost of the work actually done by now

What has actually been spent to do that work



BAC (Budget At Completion) is the total baseline budget — where the PV curve ends.

cutoff <- 8

# S-shaped ramps scaled to pass through the week-8 values in Worked Example 1.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.4 The six core metrics
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Schedule Variance} \quad SV &= EV - PV \\
\text{Cost Variance} \quad CV &= EV - AC \\
\text{Schedule Performance Index} \quad SPI &= EV / PV \\
\text{Cost Performance Index} \quad CPI &= EV / AC
\end{aligned}
\]



Reading
Schedule
Cost




Ahead / under
\(SV > 0\), \(SPI > 1\)
\(CV > 0\), \(CPI > 1\)


On plan
\(SV = 0\), \(SPI = 1\)
\(CV = 0\), \(CPI = 1\)


Behind / over
\(SV < 0\), \(SPI < 1\)
\(CV < 0\), \(CPI < 1\)




12.4.1 Worked Example 1: the RC-vehicle project at week 8
Baseline budget BAC = $620 000. By week 8 the plan said 35 % of the work should be done; 30 % is actually done; $210 000 has been spent.

BAC <- 620000
planned_pct <- 0.35
actual_pct  <- 0.30
AC <- 210000

PV <- planned_pct * BAC
EV <- actual_pct  * BAC

SV  <- EV - PV
CV  <- EV - AC
SPI <- EV / PV
CPI <- EV / AC

cat(sprintf("PV  = $%s      EV  = $%s      AC  = $%s\n",
            format(PV, big.mark = " "), format(EV, big.mark = " "),
            format(AC, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("SV  = $%s  (%s schedule)\n", format(SV, big.mark = " "),
            ifelse(SV < 0, "behind", "ahead")))
cat(sprintf("CV  = $%s  (%s budget)\n", format(CV, big.mark = " "),
            ifelse(CV < 0, "over", "under")))
cat(sprintf("SPI = %.3f   (getting %.0f cents of schedule per planned dollar)\n",
            SPI, SPI * 100))
cat(sprintf("CPI = %.3f   (getting %.0f cents of work per dollar spent)\n",
            CPI, CPI * 100))

PV  = $217 000      EV  = $186 000      AC  = $210 000
SV  = $-31 000  (behind schedule)
CV  = $-24 000  (over budget)
SPI = 0.857   (getting 86 cents of schedule per planned dollar)
CPI = 0.886   (getting 89 cents of work per dollar spent)


The project is behind schedule and over cost — and this is visible in week 8, while there is still time to act, instead of as a surprise at the end.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.5 Forecasting








Forecast
Formula
Meaning




EAC (Estimate At Completion)
\(BAC / CPI\)
Total cost if current cost efficiency holds


EAC (schedule too)
\(AC + \dfrac{BAC - EV}{CPI \times SPI}\)
If both cost and schedule performance persist


EAC (one-off overrun)
\(AC + (BAC - EV)\)
If the overrun so far was a one-time event


ETC (Estimate To Complete)
\(EAC - AC\)
Money still needed from here


VAC (Variance At Completion)
\(BAC - EAC\)
Projected total over/under budget


TCPI (To-Complete Performance Index)
\(\dfrac{BAC - EV}{BAC - AC}\)
The cost efficiency the remaining work must hit to still land on BAC




12.5.1 Try it yourself: EAC scenarios

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Which EAC formula should you actually report?

It depends on why you are over. If a one-time event caused it (a failed test you have since fixed), \(AC + (BAC - EV)\) is fair. If the overrun reflects how the team is fundamentally working (rates, productivity), \(BAC/CPI\) is the honest number. If you are also behind schedule and recovery will cost overtime, the \(CPI \times SPI\) version is the most conservative. Report the one your evidence supports — and say which assumption you made.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.6 Reading the S-curve honestly

Spend is not progress. A project can be on budget (AC ≈ PV) and badly behind (EV ≪ PV) — it just has not done the work yet.
The “watermelon” report — green on the outside, red on the inside. High-level status shows green because spend matches plan, while the earned value underneath is red.
Leading vs. lagging indicators. SPI and CPI are somewhat lagging. Leading signals — rising defect find-rate, slipping sub-milestones, key staff leaving — warn you earlier. Watch both.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.7 Integrated change control
Control only works against a meaningful baseline. Every change request goes through the same gate as in Chapter 3: assess the impact on scope, schedule, and cost; approve or reject; and if approved, re-baseline so future variance is measured against the new plan — not the old one you can no longer hit. Configuration management keeps the product definition (drawings, specs, software versions) in step with the approved baseline.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.8 Status reporting
The course’s Project Manager Report and Team Member Report templates are the reporting instruments: they roll up progress, cost, schedule, risks, and issues on a fixed cadence. Good reporting is honest (report the red while it is still fixable), consistent (same metrics every period so trends are visible), and actionable (every variance has an owner and a next step). A dashboard that only ever shows green is not a control system — it is a comfort blanket.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.9 Key Takeaways

Control is a closed loop: measure → compare to baseline → analyze variance → act, every reporting period.
Track PV (work scheduled), EV (work done), AC (money spent), all in budget dollars, against BAC.
\(SV = EV - PV\), \(CV = EV - AC\), \(SPI = EV/PV\), \(CPI = EV/AC\). Below 1 / negative = behind / over.
Forecast with EAC (\(BAC/CPI\) is the common honest form), ETC \(= EAC - AC\), VAC \(= BAC - EAC\), TCPI \(= (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC)\).
Spend is not progress. Beware the watermelon report; watch leading indicators, not just SPI/CPI.
Keep the baseline meaningful through integrated change control and configuration management.
Report honestly, consistently, and actionably — every variance gets an owner.

title: 12  Project Control Systems
text:
12.10 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Full EVM snapshot

BAC = $400 000. At the status date: PV = $180 000, EV = $150 000, AC = $165 000. Compute SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC (BAC/CPI), ETC, VAC, TCPI, and state the project’s condition in one sentence.
Solution.

BAC <- 400000; PV <- 180000; EV <- 150000; AC <- 165000
SV <- EV - PV; CV <- EV - AC; SPI <- EV / PV; CPI <- EV / AC
EAC <- BAC / CPI; ETC <- EAC - AC; VAC <- BAC - EAC
TCPI <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC)
cat(sprintf("SV=$%s  CV=$%s  SPI=%.3f  CPI=%.3f\n",
            format(SV, big.mark=" "), format(CV, big.mark=" "), SPI, CPI))
cat(sprintf("EAC=$%s  ETC=$%s  VAC=$%s  TCPI=%.3f\n",
            format(round(EAC), big.mark=" "), format(round(ETC), big.mark=" "),
            format(round(VAC), big.mark=" "), TCPI))

SV=$-30 000  CV=$-15 000  SPI=0.833  CPI=0.909
EAC=$440 000  ETC=$275 000  VAC=$-40 000  TCPI=1.064


Behind schedule (SPI 0.83) and over cost (CPI 0.91); projected to finish about $40 000 over budget, and the remaining work must run at TCPI ≈ 1.06 to still hit BAC.



Problem 2: On budget but in trouble

A project reports PV = $500 000, EV = $400 000, AC = $400 000. The sponsor sees “spend exactly matches earned value — CPI = 1.0 — we’re fine.” Are they?
Answer. Cost efficiency is fine (CPI = 1.0), but SPI = EV/PV = 0.80 — the project has completed only 80 % of the work it should have by now. It is 20 % behind schedule and will either finish late or need to spend more (overtime, added staff) to catch up, which will then push CPI below 1. This is the classic watermelon: the cost view is green, the schedule view is red.



Problem 3 (discussion): re-baseline or not?

At week 8 the RC-vehicle project is forecast (EAC) at $700 000 against a $620 000 BAC, mostly because the retailer added a second body colourway (an approved scope change) and the new line’s learning curve ran longer than planned. Should you re-baseline?
Discussion points. Split the two causes. The approved scope change is a legitimate reason to re-baseline — the extra colourway was authorised, so the budget and schedule should be formally updated and future variance measured against the new plan. The learning-curve overrun is performance against the plan, not a change to the plan — that stays as variance you must recover or explain. Re-baselining to bury performance problems (“we’ll just move the goalposts”) destroys the value of the control system; re-baselining for authorised changes keeps it honest.

Before we begin: which is harder — starting a project or finishing one?

Starting has energy and a blank page. Finishing has a tired team, a client eager to move on, and a next project already calling. Closeout is “the most difficult phase to complete effectively and has the most impact on future projects.”

title: 13  Project Closeout and Termination
text:
13.2 Introduction: planning for extinction
A defining feature of a project is a finite life. When you plan a project, you are also “planning for its extinction.” The RC-vehicle prototype project will end — and if it succeeds, its team likely rolls straight into supporting the 100 000-unit production run. That is a real, named way for a project to end, not an afterthought.
Project termination provides for:

Acceptance of the project by the sponsor
Completion of the project records
Final revision and issue of documentation to its as-built condition
Retention of the essential documentation — above all, the lessons learned

13.3 Types of termination

Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0.
ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead.








Figure 13.1: Four ways a project ends. Extinction, addition, and integration are normal; starvation is a slow, deliberate neglect.






Extinction — the project is stopped, successfully or not. The final budget is audited, team members get new assignments, material assets are dispersed or transferred per company/contract terms.
Addition — a successful project is made a formal part of the organization. An automaker that has launched a new vehicle keeps the project team on as a production support team.
Integration — the team and resources are reabsorbed into the existing structure. Common but complicated — and organizations often lose key people here, who leave for fresh project challenges rather than return to the old department.
Starvation — not really a termination act but “a willful form of neglect”: the budget is decreased slowly until the project cannot remain viable. Kept “on the books” for political reasons, a powerful sponsor’s pet project, or so it can be reactivated when budgets recover.

title: 13  Project Closeout and Termination
text:
13.4 The seven elements of closeout

close <- data.frame(
  `#` = 1:7,
  Element = c("Verify scope", "Closeout contracts", "Closeout administration",
              "Conduct a lessons-learned review", "Build a project history file",
              "Create the final project report", "Celebrate success"),
  What = c(
    "Compare to the original scope statement; resolve discrepancies; confirm every deliverable is present; assess customer satisfaction.",

    "Return all loaned personnel; complete performance evaluations.",
    "Survey everyone who was on the project; hold the meeting; be critical -- dissect what went wrong and why, not what went right.",
    "Document planned vs. actual schedule and cost (with reasons), approved changes, meeting minutes, WBS, risk plans, subcontractor and customer-satisfaction records, reviews.",
    "Document overall success, project organization, recommended changes for similar projects, techniques used to overcome obstacles, strengths and weaknesses, team recommendations, projected vs. actual impact, team members.",

  ),

Table 13.1: The seven elements of project closeout.






#
Element
What




1
Verify scope
Compare to the original scope statement; resolve discrepancies; confirm every deliverable is present; assess customer satisfaction.


2
Closeout contracts
Resolve all open issues with the customer; return or destroy proprietary documents as directed; receive final payments. The client is a future customer -- leave them feeling good.


3

13.4.1 What prevents effective closeout

Getting the project signed off discourages the other closeout activities.
The assumed urgency of every project pressures the team to cut corners on the back end.
Closeout is given low priority and easily ignored.
Lessons learned is dismissed as a bookkeeping chore.
People assume that because every project is unique, carryover is minimal.
People just want to move on to the next challenge.

title: 13  Project Closeout and Termination
text:
13.5 Project failure
Failure = the project does not deliver what was required, judged against the acceptance criteria of the sponsor and customer, and can be triggered by changes in scope, cost, or time.
Early warning signs:

Lack of viable commercial objectives
Lack of sufficient decision-making authority
Market volatility
Low priority assigned to the project

When to consider cancelling:

Costs exceed the business benefits
The project no longer meets strategic-fit criteria
Deadlines keep being missed
Technology evolves beyond the project’s scope


13.5.1 Worked Example 1: continue or cancel?
A project has already spent $480 000 (sunk). Finishing it needs another $260 000. The product, if delivered, is now worth an estimated $300 000 in benefit — the market moved while you were building.

sunk            <- 480000     # already spent -- IRRELEVANT to the decision
cost_to_finish  <- 260000
remaining_benefit <- 300000

net_if_continue <- remaining_benefit - cost_to_finish
cat(sprintf("Sunk cost (ignore it)        : $%s\n", format(sunk, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("Cost to finish               : $%s\n", format(cost_to_finish, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("Benefit if finished          : $%s\n", format(remaining_benefit, big.mark = " ")))
cat(sprintf("Net from *here*              : $%s\n", format(net_if_continue, big.mark = " ")))
cat(ifelse(net_if_continue > 0,
           "\n-> CONTINUE: the remaining benefit still beats the remaining cost.\n",
           "\n-> CANCEL: finishing loses money from here, regardless of the $480k already gone.\n"))

Sunk cost (ignore it)        : $480 000
Cost to finish               : $260 000
Benefit if finished          : $3e+05
Net from *here*              : $40 000

-> CONTINUE: the remaining benefit still beats the remaining cost.


The $480 000 is a sunk cost — it is spent whether you continue or not, so it must not enter the decision. From here, spending $260 000 to get $300 000 is still worth $40 000. (The sunk-cost fallacy — “we’ve come too far to stop” — is what keeps doomed projects alive.)

       x = "Overrun multiple", y = NULL) +

  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"),

Figure 13.2: Cost overrun as a multiple of the original budget for three well-documented failures. Project Taurus (London Stock Exchange) ran to roughly 132 times its first budget before being abandoned after 11 years.






Bank of America “MasterNet” (1984) — trust-department automation. Over budget by $35M, rising toward $80M; a 1988 failure meant loss of control over billions in trust accounts, all eventually recovered, but the entire 255-person department was let go as depositors fled. Cause: scope and complexity understood far too late.
Future Imagery Architecture (US spy satellites, 1997) — bid won by a contractor that had never built an imaging satellite; internal estimate already predicted a $4B overrun. Testing was cut to save money; a subcontractor’s undisclosed manufacturing change caused gyroscope defects undiscovered for three years; costs reached ~$18B by 2005. Cause: unqualified bidder, cut testing, uncontrolled change.
Canadian Firearms Registry (1995) — estimated at $119M to implement; a 2002 audit projected ~$1B. Causes: scope not understood, no plan for inter-agency cooperation, inconsistent data criteria, cost cover-up, no measurement of whether the registry actually worked.
Channel Tunnel (budgeted 1979, opened 1994, one year late) — final cost roughly double the original budget.
Project Taurus (London Stock Exchange paperless settlement, 1983) — abandoned after 11 years at ~132 times its original budget after switching to an incompatible US system that clashed with British finance law.

The recurring threads: scope not truly understood; optimism and cost concealment; cutting testing to save money; no plan for the interfaces between organizations; and pressing on past every off-ramp because of sunk cost.

13.7 Closing out the RC-vehicle project

Verify scope against the signed scope statement: all body options delivered, drop and EMC tests passed, compliance approvals in hand, retailer satisfaction confirmed.
Closeout contracts: settle final invoices with MCS/Paragon and the carbon-fibre supplier; return the customer’s proprietary artwork.
Administration: return the borrowed design engineers and millwrights to their functional managers with completed performance reviews.
Lessons learned: the new-line learning curve and the unproven-supplier risk are the two entries that matter most for the next program.
Termination by addition: the prototype team transitions into the production support team for the 100 000-unit run.
Celebrate — away from the plant, with everyone who contributed.

title: 13  Project Closeout and Termination
text:
13.8 Key Takeaways

Termination provides sponsor acceptance, complete records, as-built documentation, and retained lessons learned.
Types: extinction (stopped), addition (becomes permanent), integration (reabsorbed), starvation (slow deliberate neglect).
Work the seven elements: verify scope, close contracts, close administration, lessons learned, history file, final report, celebrate.
Closeout fails because sign-off feels like “done”, the next project is louder, and lessons learned is treated as bookkeeping. Resist all three.
Cancel when the cost to complete exceeds the remaining benefit — the money already spent is sunk and irrelevant to that decision.
Famous failures share the same causes: scope not understood, cost concealed, testing cut, interfaces unplanned, sunk-cost momentum.

title: 13  Project Closeout and Termination
text:
13.9 Practice Problems


Problem 1: Sunk cost trap

A project has consumed $1.2M of a $1.5M budget. Finishing needs $500 000 (the last $300 000 of budget plus a $200 000 overrun). The delivered product is now worth $350 000. The sponsor says “we’ve spent $1.2M — we can’t stop now.” Evaluate.
Solution.

cost_to_finish <- 500000
remaining_benefit <- 350000
cat(sprintf("Net from here: $%s - $%s = $%s\n",
            format(remaining_benefit, big.mark = " "),
            format(cost_to_finish, big.mark = " "),
            format(remaining_benefit - cost_to_finish, big.mark = " ")))

Net from here: $350 000 - $5e+05 = $-150 000


Finishing turns $500 000 of new spend into $350 000 of value — a $150 000 loss from today. The $1.2M is gone either way. Cancel (or de-scope until the remaining cost drops below $350 000). “We can’t stop now” is the sunk-cost fallacy.



Problem 2: Which termination type?


The RC-vehicle prototype team becomes the production line’s support team. → Addition.
A cancelled R&D project’s engineers return to the design department. → Integration.
A failed pilot is shut down, its budget audited, its test rig sold. → Extinction.
A VP’s favourite project keeps a $1/year budget so it stays “active” on paper. → Starvation.




Problem 3 (discussion): the team wants to skip lessons learned

The RC-vehicle project delivered late and over budget but the product passed. The exhausted team wants to skip the lessons-learned review and start on the production ramp. As PM, what do you do and why?
Discussion points. This is exactly the moment the review matters most — a troubled project is where the carryover value is highest, and the next program will hit the same new-line learning curve and same supplier risk. Keep it short and structured, focus on what went wrong and why (not blame), capture 2–3 concrete, assigned actions, and put it in the history file before the team disperses and the memory fades. Skipping it guarantees the next project repeats the overrun.
